old definition: A clarifying phrase used when a debate about creative or messaging is actually about something deeper — the brand's fundamental place in the market. It redirects tactical conversations to the strategic level.
new definition: A way to say a choice is about the brand's place, not one advert.
old example: The team was arguing about which tagline to use. Riley stopped them: That is a positioning decision, not a campaign decision. We cannot choose a tagline until we agree on what we want to be known for. Let's go back one step.
new example: Changing our price is a positioning decision, not a campaign decision.

old definition: A mindset and method focused on finding fast, creative ways to grow — often with limited budget. Growth hackers test ideas quickly, cut what fails, and scale what works.
new definition: Finding fast, cheap and creative ways to grow.
old example: Riley said: Growth hacking is not about tricks — it is about speed and discipline. You test ten ideas, nine fail, one doubles your sign-ups. Then you put everything behind that one. That is the whole game.
new example: Free invites to friends was our best growth hacking idea.

old definition: A framework for measuring growth across five stages — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, and Revenue. The acronym AARRR sounds like a pirate, which is where the name comes from.
new definition: Five steps used to measure a company's growth.
old example: Marcus said: I keep hearing about pirate metrics. Riley said: AARRR — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue. It is a simple way to find where your funnel is leaking. Most companies focus on acquisition and ignore retention. That is the most expensive mistake you can make.
new example: We use pirate metrics to see where users leave.

old definition: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — the five stages of the growth funnel. Each stage is a place where users can drop off, and each one needs a different strategy to improve.
new definition: Short for acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue.
old example: Riley said: Walk me through your AARRR numbers. Where are you losing people? Marcus said: Activation. People sign up but fewer than 20% complete the onboarding. Riley said: That is where you start — not more acquisition. Fix the hole in your bucket first.
new example: AARRR helps us check each step of growth.

old definition: A growth mechanism where existing users bring in new users — who then bring in more. A strong viral loop means every new user helps you acquire the next one, reducing your overall cost of growth.
new definition: When users bring new users, who then bring more users.
old example: Riley explained: Dropbox built their viral loop into the product. You get more storage when you invite a friend. The friend signs up, and they also want more storage, so they invite their friends. One user becomes ten. That is a viral loop at its best.
new example: Our 'invite a friend' button created a viral loop.

old definition: A growth strategy where the product itself is the main driver of acquisition, retention, and expansion — instead of sales or marketing. Users experience the value of the product and then buy or invite others.
new definition: Growth that comes mainly from people using the product.
old example: Marcus asked: Why does Slack grow so fast without a big sales team? Riley said: Product-led growth. When you use Slack and love it, you invite your whole team. The product does the selling. Marketing and sales support the motion — they do not drive it.
new example: Our free plan drives product-led growth.

old definition: The point at which a new user first experiences the real value of a product — the 'aha moment'. If users do not reach activation quickly, they leave before they become loyal customers.
new definition: The moment a new user first sees the value of a product.
old example: Riley said: Activation is the most underinvested stage in most funnels. You spend all your budget getting people in the door, and then you let them wander around and leave. Find the one action that predicts long-term retention — and get every new user there in the first session.
new example: Activation happens when a user sends their first invoice.

old definition: A structured process of testing ideas to find what works. In growth marketing, experimentation means running fast, controlled tests — changing one variable at a time — and using the results to make better decisions.
new definition: Testing ideas to see what works.
old example: Riley said to the team: Growth is built on experimentation. You do not have to know the answer — you have to be disciplined about finding it. We run ten experiments a month. We expect eight to fail. That is not a bad result — that is a healthy growth culture.
new example: Experimentation helped us find the best price.

old definition: Keeping customers coming back after their first purchase or sign-up. Strong retention means users keep using, paying, and engaging over time — and it is almost always cheaper than acquiring new ones.
new definition: Keeping customers coming back.
old example: Marcus asked: Should we focus on acquisition or retention? Riley said: If your retention is below 40% at 30 days, focus on retention. You are filling a leaking bucket. Fix the leak first — then turn on the tap.
new example: Our retention is high: most users stay for a year.

old definition: The key diagnostic question in growth marketing — asking which stage of the AARRR funnel is losing users. Identifying the leak is the first step to fixing it.
new definition: A question about where you are losing customers.
old example: Riley opened the growth review: Before we talk about new channels, let's answer one question — where is the funnel leaking? Show me the drop-off at each stage. The answer to that question tells us exactly where to focus.
new example: Sales are low. Where is the funnel leaking?

word: We need to find the aha moment
old definition: The moment when a new user first understands the value of a product. Finding and shortening the path to the aha moment is one of the most powerful things a growth team can do.
new definition: A way to say we must find when users first love the product.
old example: Riley said: Our activation rate is 18%. That tells me users are not reaching the aha moment before they leave. We need to find it — what is the one thing our best customers do in the first session that casual users never do? That is the aha moment. Get everyone there faster.
new example: We need to find the aha moment for new users.

word: Let's run an experiment on that
old definition: A growth team phrase that turns an idea or assumption into a structured test. It signals that decisions should be based on data, not opinions.
new definition: A way to suggest testing an idea.
old example: The team was debating whether to change the onboarding flow. Riley said: We do not have to guess — let's run an experiment on that. We test two versions with 50% of new users each. In two weeks we have a real answer.
new example: Good idea. Let's run an experiment on that next week.

word: Double down on what is working
old definition: To invest more in a strategy, channel, or tactic that is already showing strong results. In growth marketing, this means scaling experiments that win — and stopping the ones that do not.
new definition: To put more effort into what already works.
old example: Riley said after the monthly review: Referral is generating 40% of our new sign-ups at one third of the acquisition cost. That is the signal. We need to double down on what is working — more budget, more resource, a dedicated team on referral. Everything else waits.
new example: Video works well, so let's double down on what is working.

old definition: A specific metric used to measure how many new users each existing user brings in. A viral coefficient above 1 means the product is growing on its own — every user brings in more than one new user.
new definition: A way to say how many new users each user brings.
old example: Riley said: Our viral coefficient is 0.4. Marcus asked: Is that good? Riley said: It means every ten users bring in four more. That is not viral — it is a nice bonus. To get truly viral growth, we need to get above 1. That is the threshold where growth becomes self-sustaining.
new example: The viral coefficient is 1.2, so we are growing.

word: Fix the retention before you scale acquisition
old definition: A core growth principle — you cannot grow sustainably if users are leaving as fast as they arrive. Fixing retention first means every new user you acquire stays longer and is worth more.
new definition: A rule to keep users before you look for more.
old example: The team wanted to triple the paid acquisition budget. Riley said: I hear you — but fix the retention before you scale acquisition. Right now we are spending £50 to get a user who stays for three weeks. If we fix retention first, that same £50 gets us a user who stays for six months. The economics change completely.
new example: Fix the retention before you scale acquisition, or you waste money.

old definition: The question that turns a data point into an insight. 'So what?' asks: why does this number matter? What does it mean for the business? Every data slide needs a clear answer to this question.
new definition: A question that asks why a fact matters.
old example: Riley looked at Marcus's slide: Conversion rate is up 3%. Riley said: So what? What does that mean in revenue terms? What caused it? What should we do next? If your audience is asking these questions, the story is not done yet.
new example: Sales went up 5%. So what? Is that good?

old definition: A storytelling framework that starts with the recommendation at the top, supported by key insights, each supported by data. It is designed for busy audiences who want the answer first, not the analysis.
new definition: A way to start with the main idea and add details below it.
old example: Riley said: Busy executives do not want to watch you build to the conclusion. Use the insight pyramid — give them the recommendation first, then the three insights that support it, then the data underneath. Answer first, evidence second.
new example: She used an insight pyramid, starting with her main point.

old definition: The story built around data — connecting numbers, insights, and implications into a logical sequence that leads to a clear conclusion. A data narrative is not a data dump — it is a structured argument.
new definition: A story that explains what the numbers mean.
old example: Marcus said: I have 40 slides of data. Riley said: That is not a data narrative — that is a report. A narrative has a beginning, a middle, and an end. It has tension and resolution. What is the one thing you want the audience to believe when you finish?
new example: His data narrative made the report easy to follow.

old definition: The way data is displayed — as a chart, graph, table, or diagram. Good visualisation makes a pattern obvious in seconds. Bad visualisation makes people stare at a slide and still not understand.
new definition: A chart or picture that shows data.
old example: Riley said: A bar chart comparing five numbers is clear. A table with 40 rows is not — that is a data dump, not a visualisation. The test of a good visualisation is whether someone can understand the point in under five seconds without you explaining it.
new example: This visualisation shows sales by country.

old definition: A conclusion drawn from data — going beyond what the numbers say directly to explain what they mean or predict what comes next. In data storytelling, inference is how you turn observation into insight.
new definition: A conclusion you reach from the facts.
old example: Riley said: The data shows churn went up in Q3 and NPS dropped in Q2. The inference is that the satisfaction problem in Q2 caused the churn in Q3 — they are connected. That is the insight. Now we know where to focus.
new example: My inference is that young people prefer video.

old definition: The single most important number that summarises the state of a business or campaign. A good headline metric is simple, meaningful, and immediately understood by a non-expert audience.
new definition: The most important number in a report.
old example: Riley said: Your board does not want 20 metrics. They want one headline metric — the number that tells them if the business is healthy or not. For us, that is monthly active users. Everything else is context.
new example: Our headline metric is monthly sales.

old definition: The difference between two things happening at the same time (correlation) and one thing causing the other (causation). Confusing them leads to wrong conclusions and bad decisions.
new definition: The difference between things happening together and one causing the other.
old example: Marcus said: Ice cream sales and drowning rates both go up in summer — does ice cream cause drowning? Riley said: No — that is correlation, not causation. Both go up because of hot weather. When you present data, always ask: are we observing a pattern or explaining a cause?
new example: Remember correlation vs causation: more ads did not cause the rain.

old definition: Comparing your results to an external standard — such as an industry average, a competitor, or a previous period. Without benchmarking, a number has no context and no meaning.
new definition: Comparing your results with others.
old example: Riley said: Our open rate is 22%. Is that good? Without benchmarking, I cannot tell you. Against an industry average of 18%, it is great. Against our top competitor who is at 35%, it is a problem. Context changes everything.
new example: Benchmarking shows we are above the industry average.

word: The story the data is telling us is...
old definition: A phrase that frames data as a narrative rather than a collection of numbers. It signals that you have done the analytical work and are now presenting a clear conclusion, not a data dump.
new definition: A way to explain what the numbers mean.
old example: Riley opened her presentation: I am not going to walk you through every number. The story the data is telling us is this: we are winning on acquisition but losing on retention — and retention is where the revenue lives. That is the problem we need to solve.
new example: The story the data is telling us is that email works best.

word: What this means for the business is...
old definition: A connecting phrase that turns a data observation into a business implication. It is the 'so what' made explicit — bridging the gap between the number and the decision.
new definition: A way to explain why a fact matters.
old example: Riley said: NPS dropped 8 points in Q2. What this means for the business is that churn will increase in Q3 unless we act now. That is the implication. The data is the evidence. The action is what we decide today.
new example: What this means for the business is more profit.

word: Let me give you the headline first
old definition: A signal that you are structuring your presentation using the insight pyramid — answer first, evidence second. It shows you understand that your audience wants the conclusion before the analysis.
new definition: A way to say the main point before the details.
old example: Riley said: Let me give you the headline first — our customer acquisition cost has increased by 40% and our payback period is now 18 months. That is the problem. Now let me show you the three reasons that explains why and what we recommend.
new example: Let me give you the headline first: we beat our target.

word: The inference we draw from this is...
old definition: A phrase that signals you are moving from data observation to analytical conclusion. It is what separates a data presenter from a strategic thinker.
new definition: A way to share a conclusion from the data.
old example: Riley said: Engagement dropped 30% in the week we changed the homepage. The inference we draw from this is that the new design is hurting discovery. That is a hypothesis, not a certainty — but it is where we look first.
new example: The inference we draw from this is that price matters most.

word: We need to be careful about correlation versus causation here
old definition: A phrase that signals analytical discipline — warning the audience not to assume that because two things happened at the same time, one caused the other.
new definition: A warning not to think one thing caused another too quickly.
old example: Marcus said: Sales went up 20% in the same month we launched the campaign. Riley said: We need to be careful about correlation versus causation here. Did the campaign drive the sales, or was there a seasonal factor? We need the controlled data before we claim credit.
new example: We need to be careful about correlation versus causation here.

old definition: A phrase used to add benchmarking or comparative data that gives a number meaning. Without context, a number is just a number — this phrase is how you make it a story.
new definition: A way to compare a number so it is easier to understand.
old example: Riley said: Our churn rate is 5% per month. To put that in context — the industry average is 2%. We are losing customers at more than twice the rate of our competitors. That context is what turns a number into an urgent problem.
new example: To put that in context, the average is only 2%.

old definition: Adapting marketing content for a new market so that it has the same emotional impact — not just the same words. Transcreation goes beyond translation to recreate the feeling, humour, or cultural reference that makes a campaign work.
new definition: Changing an advert for a new country so it keeps the same feeling.
old example: Riley said: Translation gives you the words. Transcreation gives you the effect. If a tagline is funny in English because of a wordplay that does not exist in Portuguese, translation will give you a flat sentence. Transcreation will find a new way to make someone in São Paulo laugh.
new example: The joke needed transcreation, not just translation.

old definition: The ability to understand how cultural differences affect communication, behaviour, and decision-making — and to use that understanding to work more effectively across cultures.
new definition: Understanding how cultures are different.
old example: Marcus said: Why did the campaign perform so differently in Japan versus Germany? Riley said: Cultural intelligence. Direct, bold claims work in some cultures. In others, humility and understatement perform better. Understanding that difference before you shoot the creative saves the budget and the relationship.
new example: Good cultural intelligence stops big mistakes in new markets.

old definition: The process of adjusting a campaign's content, format, or messaging for a specific region — while keeping the brand strategy consistent. Regional adaptation is different from transcreation: it covers everything from imagery to channel selection to offer structure.
new definition: Changing a campaign to suit one region.
old example: Riley said: Regional adaptation is not just changing the language. It might mean choosing different spokespeople, different visual references, or even a different offer structure. In some markets, a discount drives action. In others, exclusivity works better.
new example: The Asian campaign needed some regional adaptation.

old definition: Following the laws, regulations, and standards that govern advertising and marketing in each market. What is legal in one country may be restricted or banned in another — compliance protects the brand and avoids legal risk.
new definition: Following the rules and laws.
old example: Riley warned the team: Before we launch in France, we need compliance sign-off. Comparative advertising is highly regulated there. What we can say about competitors in the UK, we cannot say in France without specific evidence and legal approval.
new example: Every advert must pass a compliance check.

old definition: Adapting a product, campaign, or piece of content for a local market — including language, format, currency, date style, imagery, and cultural references. Localisation is broader than translation and deeper than adaptation.
new definition: Changing a product or message for a local market.
old example: Marcus said: We localised the campaign for the UAE — not just the language, but the imagery, the pricing in dirhams, the timing around Ramadan, and the channel mix. That is real localisation, not just running the English campaign with Arabic subtitles.
new example: Localisation means local prices, language and photos.

old definition: Presenting the same core identity, values, and visual language across all markets — even when the execution changes. Without brand consistency, customers in different countries experience different brands.
new definition: Keeping a brand the same in every place.
old example: Riley said: We can adapt the message for each market. But the logo, the colour palette, the tone of voice — those do not change. Brand consistency is what makes us recognisable in São Paulo and Singapore. Execution varies. Identity does not.
new example: Brand consistency means the same logo in every country.

old definition: A document that defines the strategy, objectives, and brand guidelines for a campaign that will run across multiple markets. The global brief is the foundation — regional teams adapt from it, not away from it.
new definition: A document with the main plan for all countries.
old example: Riley said: Every global campaign starts with a global brief. It defines what we are trying to say, who we are saying it to, and what the brand experience must feel like — regardless of language or market. Regional teams take that brief and build their version within it.
new example: The global brief sets the colours and the main message.

old definition: A visual tool that shows where performance is strongest and weakest across markets, regions, or audience segments. In global campaign management, a heatmap helps identify where to invest more and where to investigate problems.
new definition: A coloured chart that shows where results are strong or weak.
old example: Riley showed the global performance review: Look at the heatmap — green across Western Europe, red across Southeast Asia, and yellow in Latin America. That tells us exactly where to focus the next 30 days of optimisation effort.
new example: The heatmap shows that Spain is our weakest market.

word: We need to transcreate, not just translate
old definition: A core principle of global campaign management — a direct instruction to adapt for emotional impact rather than just converting words. It is used when a translation would be technically accurate but culturally flat or ineffective.
new definition: A way to say the message must feel right, not just be in a new language.
old example: Riley looked at the translated tagline and said: This is technically correct but it lands completely flat in Spanish. We need to transcreate, not just translate. Get a native creative team in Madrid to give us something that works culturally — same feeling, different execution.
new example: This slogan won't work in Japan. We need to transcreate, not just translate.

old definition: A standard question in global campaign management before any content goes live. It ensures that marketing materials have been reviewed for legal and regulatory requirements in each specific market.
new definition: A question to check that something follows the rules.
old example: Before the team signed off on the campaign for Germany, Riley asked: Has this been through compliance? The claims we make about performance need substantiation under German advertising law. We do not launch until legal has cleared it.
new example: Before we post it, has this been through compliance?

word: What is the global brief saying on this?
old definition: A phrase used to redirect a regional debate back to the agreed global strategy. It reminds teams that the brief is the authority — regional preferences should not override strategic decisions made at the global level.
new definition: A question to check the main plan.
old example: The regional team wanted to use a different brand colour for their market. Riley said: What is the global brief saying on this? The visual identity is fixed — it is one of the non-negotiables. We can adapt the creative concept, but not the brand elements.
new example: We disagree on colours. What is the global brief saying on this?

word: What does the local team say?
old definition: A prompt to gather on-the-ground cultural intelligence before making a campaign decision for a specific market. It signals that global teams respect local expertise and do not impose decisions without consultation.
new definition: A question to ask people in that country for advice.
old example: Riley said before the Southeast Asia launch: What does the local team say about the imagery? The global creative uses direct eye contact, which can read as aggressive in some markets there. I want their sign-off on this before we brief the media buy.
new example: Before we choose the photo, what does the local team say?

word: Build in regional flexibility from the start
old definition: A design principle for global campaigns — planning from the outset for the campaign to be adapted, not assuming the global version will work everywhere. It saves time, budget, and creative rework later.
new definition: A way to say plan for local changes early.
old example: Riley briefed the creative agency: Build in regional flexibility from the start. Design the campaign so that the hero image, the tagline, and the offer can all be swapped out by regional teams without rebuilding the whole thing. Flexibility is not a weakness — it is a structural requirement.
new example: Build in regional flexibility from the start, so each country can adapt.

word: Where are we seeing the biggest performance gap across markets?
old definition: A diagnostic question for global campaign reviews — identifying which markets are underperforming relative to the benchmark and investigating why. It is the first step in global optimisation.
new definition: A question about which country is doing worst.
old example: Riley opened the quarterly review: Let's look at the heatmap. Where are we seeing the biggest performance gap across markets? Southeast Asia is red — conversion is 40% below the global average. That is our focus for Q3. I want a local team debrief before we make any changes.
new example: Where are we seeing the biggest performance gap across markets?

old definition: A plan that shows how a major change will happen over time — what will be done, in what order, and by when. A transformation roadmap keeps everyone aligned and makes a complex change feel manageable.
new definition: A plan that shows the steps of a big change over time.
old example: Riley said: We cannot transform the whole marketing function in one quarter. Here is the transformation roadmap — three phases over 18 months. Phase one: people and process. Phase two: data and technology. Phase three: scale and optimise. Each phase has clear outputs and a review gate.
new example: Our transformation roadmap has three stages over two years.

old definition: The process of helping people in an organisation understand, accept, and adapt to a major change. Without change management, even the best strategy fails because the people who need to execute it do not get on board.
new definition: Helping people accept and adapt to a change at work.
old example: Marcus said: We announced the new system last month and adoption is only 30%. Riley said: That is a change management problem, not a technology problem. People do not resist change — they resist losing control, clarity, and confidence. You have to address all three.
new example: Good change management made the new system easy for the team.

old definition: A way of working that breaks marketing work into short, focused cycles — called sprints — where teams plan, execute, and review quickly. Agile marketing prioritises speed, learning, and adaptability over long, fixed plans.
new definition: Working in short, quick cycles and changing plans often.
old example: Riley said: Agile marketing is not about moving fast and breaking things. It is about moving fast and learning things. Short sprints, clear priorities, daily communication, and a commitment to changing direction when the data says so. That is the discipline.
new example: With agile marketing, we change our ads every two weeks.

old definition: A fixed, short period of work — usually one to four weeks — in which a team focuses on a defined set of tasks. At the end of each sprint, the team reviews what was achieved and plans the next one.
new definition: A short period of work with one clear goal.
old example: Marcus asked: How do we manage our campaign work in sprints? Riley said: Each sprint has a goal — one thing we are trying to achieve or learn. We plan it on Monday, we execute through the week, and we review on Friday. What worked, what failed, what changes next sprint. Simple.
new example: This sprint, we will finish the new landing page.

old definition: The agreement and support of the key people whose approval or participation is needed for a change to succeed. Without stakeholder buy-in, transformation stalls — either from resistance, budget cuts, or withdrawal of support.
new definition: Support from the important people in a project.
old example: Riley said: Before we start the transformation, I need stakeholder buy-in from three people — the CFO on budget, the CTO on technology, and the CEO on strategic priority. If any of those three are not aligned, we will hit a wall in month two.
new example: We need stakeholder buy-in before we change the team.

old definition: The difference between the skills, tools, or processes a team currently has and what they need to achieve the transformation goal. Identifying capability gaps is the first step in building a credible change plan.
new definition: The difference between the skills you have and the skills you need.
old example: Riley presented the audit: Here is the capability gap. Our team is strong in brand and content but has almost no data literacy or performance marketing experience. To run the new model, we need to close that gap — through hiring, training, or agency support. Probably all three.
new example: Our biggest capability gap is data skills.

old definition: The way a team or organisation is structured to deliver its work — including roles, processes, tools, and decision-making. Transformation almost always requires changing the operating model, not just the strategy.
new definition: How a team is set up to do its work.
old example: Riley said: The strategy is right. The problem is the operating model. We have too many approval layers, the wrong team structure for agile work, and tools that do not connect. Changing the strategy without changing the operating model is like installing a new engine in a car with no wheels.
new example: Our new operating model has smaller teams.

old definition: The degree to which a marketing team or organisation uses digital tools, data, and ways of working effectively. Low digital maturity means teams rely on intuition and manual processes. High digital maturity means decisions are data-driven and execution is automated where possible.
new definition: How well a team uses digital tools and data.
old example: Riley said: Our digital maturity assessment shows we are at stage two out of five — we have the tools but we are not using them well. The transformation goal is to reach stage four in 18 months — where decisions are driven by data and the team can execute campaigns without constant manual effort.
new example: Our digital maturity is low, so we still use paper reports.

word: Where are we on the roadmap?
old definition: A progress check phrase used in transformation projects. It asks which phase, milestone, or deliverable has been completed relative to the plan — and whether the project is on track.
new definition: A question to check progress on a plan.
old example: Riley opened the quarterly review: Where are we on the roadmap? Phase one was due to complete in March. I want to know what is done, what is delayed, and what is at risk. Then we make a decision about whether to adjust the plan or accelerate.
new example: It's been six months. Where are we on the roadmap?

word: We need to bring people with us
old definition: A change management principle — change fails when it is imposed on people without explanation or involvement. 'Bringing people with you' means communicating clearly, involving teams in the process, and addressing concerns before they become resistance.
new definition: A way to say the team must support the change.
old example: Riley said to the leadership team: The strategy is excellent. But we need to bring people with us. If the team hears about the transformation through a slide deck, they will resist it. Get them in the room early. Show them what is changing, what is staying the same, and why this matters for them.
new example: This is a big change, so we need to bring people with us.

word: What is the sprint goal this week?
old definition: The question that opens every sprint in an agile marketing team. It defines the one thing the team is trying to achieve or learn in the coming period — and everything else is secondary.
new definition: A question about the main task for a short work period.
old example: Riley opened the Monday planning session: What is the sprint goal this week? Not a list of tasks — one outcome. If we achieve this one thing by Friday, the week is a success. Marcus said: Test whether shorter email subject lines improve open rates in our B2B list. Riley said: Perfect. Everything else supports that.
new example: Before we start, what is the sprint goal this week?

word: Close the capability gap before you scale
old definition: A transformation principle — scaling a broken model makes the problems bigger, not smaller. Before expanding, make sure the team has the skills, tools, and processes needed to execute well.
new definition: A rule to learn the skills you need before you grow.
old example: The CEO asked Riley to double the marketing headcount before the transformation was complete. Riley said: We need to close the capability gap before we scale. Hiring more people into a broken model just gives us more people doing the wrong things. Let me show you what we need to fix first.
new example: Close the capability gap before you scale, or things will break.

word: What needs to change in the operating model?
old definition: A diagnostic question asked during transformation — identifying which structural, process, or role changes are needed to make the new strategy actually work.
new definition: A question about how the team should be set up.
old example: After the strategy was approved, Riley asked the team: What needs to change in the operating model? We have a new strategy but the same approval layers, the same team structure, and the same tool stack. Strategy without operating model change is just a document.
new example: The team is too slow. What needs to change in the operating model?

old definition: A change management principle — the earlier key stakeholders are involved, the less likely they are to resist or block the change later. Early involvement creates ownership, not just awareness.
new definition: A rule to get support from key people at the start.
old example: Riley said: My biggest mistake in the last transformation was announcing the change and then asking for support. Get stakeholder buy-in early — ideally before the plan is finalised. Let them shape it. People support what they help to build.
new example: Get stakeholder buy-in early, so the project doesn't stop later.

old definition: A contractual agreement that prevents one or both parties from working with competitors. Exclusivity can protect a partnership — but it limits flexibility and must be negotiated carefully.
new definition: An agreement that you will only work with one partner.
old example: The agency proposed a 12-month exclusivity clause. Riley said: I understand why you want it — but I cannot agree to exclusivity across all marketing services. I am open to exclusivity within a defined scope — performance media only. Outside that, we need to be able to bring in specialist partners.
new example: They want exclusivity, so we can't work with their competitors.

old definition: A contractual agreement where one party agrees to cover the costs, losses, or legal liabilities of the other if something goes wrong. Indemnity clauses protect each party from the mistakes or failures of the other.
new definition: A promise to pay for losses if something goes wrong.
old example: Riley said: The indemnity clause in their contract says we are responsible for any third-party IP claims arising from content they create for us. That is backwards. They are creating the content — the indemnity should run the other way. Get legal to flag this before we sign.
new example: The indemnity protects us if the agency breaks the law.

old definition: Service Level Agreement — a contract that defines the minimum level of service a vendor must deliver. SLAs include response times, delivery timelines, uptime guarantees, and what happens if those standards are not met.
new definition: Short for service level agreement: the minimum service a partner promises.
old example: Riley said: The SLA needs to be specific. 'Best efforts' is not an SLA — it is an excuse. I want 48-hour response times on all campaign queries, a 99.5% platform uptime guarantee, and clear escalation procedures if either of those is missed.
new example: Our SLA says they must reply within four hours.

old definition: A section of a contract that ties payment, continuation, or other terms to specific measurable results. Performance clauses protect the client by ensuring the vendor is incentivised to deliver — not just to be present.
new definition: A part of a contract that links payment to results.
old example: Riley said: We need a performance clause in the agency contract. If they do not hit the agreed cost-per-lead target by Q2, the retainer reduces by 20%. That is not punitive — it is aligned. We both win when the campaigns work.
new example: The performance clause pays them more for more sales.

old definition: A section of a contract that defines the conditions under which either party can end the agreement — including notice periods, penalties, and what happens to work in progress.
new definition: A part of a contract that explains how to end it.
old example: Riley reviewed the contract: There is no exit clause. That means we are locked in for 24 months with no way out if performance is poor or if our strategy changes. I will not sign without a 90-day exit clause with no penalty if SLA targets are missed for three consecutive months.
new example: The exit clause lets us leave with three months' notice.

old definition: A fixed monthly fee paid to an agency or consultant in exchange for an agreed scope of work or availability. A retainer provides predictable cost but requires clear scope definition to avoid scope creep.
new definition: A fixed monthly fee for ongoing work.
old example: Riley said: We pay the agency a monthly retainer of £25,000. In return, they handle all paid social, weekly reporting, and campaign management. If they want to add services, the retainer goes up — and that needs a change order, not an email.
new example: We pay the agency a retainer of £5,000 a month.

old definition: A detailed description of what a vendor or partner will deliver — including deliverables, timelines, responsibilities, and what is explicitly excluded. A clear scope of work prevents scope creep and disputes.
new definition: A list of exactly what a partner will do.
old example: Marcus said: The agency keeps adding things to our project. Riley said: That is scope creep and it is a contract problem. Your scope of work should list exactly what is included and what requires a separate agreement. Send it back to them with a change order for everything that was not in the original scope.
new example: The scope of work includes four videos and ten posts.

old definition: The maximum amount one party can be required to pay the other in the event of a loss or breach of contract. A liability cap protects both sides from disproportionate financial exposure.
new definition: The most money one side must pay if something goes wrong.
old example: Riley said: Their proposed liability cap is one month of fees. For a campaign that generates millions in revenue, that is completely inadequate. Negotiate it up to twelve months — or link it to the actual value at risk rather than an arbitrary fee multiple.
new example: The liability cap is one year of fees.

word: I am not comfortable with that clause
old definition: A professional, non-aggressive way to signal disagreement with a specific contract term. It opens a negotiation without creating conflict — and signals that you have read the contract carefully.
new definition: A polite way to say you don't agree with part of a contract.
old example: The vendor presented the final contract. Riley read it and said: I am not comfortable with that clause — specifically the 24-month lock-in with no exit rights. That is a significant commitment without adequate protection for us if performance does not meet expectations. Can we discuss alternatives?
new example: I am not comfortable with that clause about price increases.

word: We need to define the scope more tightly
old definition: A phrase used when the scope of work in a contract is too vague and could lead to disputes or scope creep. It signals that you want clear, specific deliverables before signing.
new definition: A way to say the work must be described more clearly.
old example: Riley said: Before we agree on the retainer, we need to define the scope more tightly. Right now it says 'marketing support services' — that could mean anything. I want a defined list of deliverables, response time commitments, and a clear process for anything that falls outside it.
new example: We need to define the scope more tightly to avoid extra costs.

word: What happens if you miss the SLA?
old definition: A direct negotiation question that establishes the consequences of underdelivery. A well-negotiated SLA is not just a target — it has specific, agreed consequences if the standard is not met.
new definition: A question about the result of poor service.
old example: Riley asked the technology vendor: What happens if you miss the SLA? The contract says 99.5% uptime — but there is no remedy clause. I want to know: if uptime drops below that threshold, what is the credit, what is the escalation path, and after how many misses do I have the right to exit?
new example: What happens if you miss the SLA? Do we get money back?

old definition: A negotiation proposal that links the vendor's payment to specific results — rather than just activity. It aligns incentives and ensures the vendor is motivated by the same outcomes as the client.
new definition: A suggestion to pay more for better results.
old example: Riley said: I want to propose a different fee structure. Let's tie compensation to performance. Base retainer at £15,000, and a bonus structure linked to hitting the cost-per-lead target. If you hit it, you earn more. If you miss it, we pay less. That is alignment, not punishment.
new example: Let's tie compensation to performance and pay per lead.

word: What is your position on exclusivity?
old definition: An open negotiation question that invites the other party to explain their exclusivity requirements — before you reveal your own position. It helps you understand what they need before making an offer.
new definition: A question about whether a partner wants to work only with you.
old example: Before responding to the agency's proposed exclusivity clause, Riley asked: What is your position on exclusivity? Why is it important to you? I want to understand the concern before we discuss terms. That conversation revealed the agency was worried about knowledge transfer to competitors — which gave Riley a narrower way to address it.
new example: Before we sign, what is your position on exclusivity?

word: That is a deal-breaker for us
old definition: A clear, professional statement that a specific term is non-negotiable — the deal will not proceed if it remains unchanged. It should be used sparingly and only when the position is genuine.
new definition: A way to say you cannot accept something at all.
old example: The vendor refused to include an exit clause. Riley said: That is a deal-breaker for us. We cannot commit to a 24-month contract with no exit rights — our board will not approve it and I will not sign it. We need either a performance-linked exit or a 90-day notice period. Which can you offer?
new example: A two-year contract is a deal-breaker for us.

old definition: The method used to decide which marketing touchpoint gets credit for a conversion. Different attribution models give credit to the first touchpoint, the last touchpoint, or distribute it across multiple touchpoints.
new definition: A way to decide which ad or channel gets credit for a sale.
old example: Riley said: Last-click attribution gives 100% of the credit to the final ad a customer clicked before buying. But if they saw six touchpoints over three weeks, last click is telling you the wrong story. Your attribution model determines what you optimise for — and what you cut.
new example: Our attribution model gives all the credit to the last click.

old definition: An attribution approach that gives credit to multiple touchpoints across the customer journey — not just the first or last. It gives a more accurate picture of how different channels work together to drive conversion.
new definition: Giving credit to every ad a customer saw before buying.
old example: Marcus asked: Why is email getting so little budget if it drives 20% of conversions? Riley said: Because we are using last-click attribution. Email is rarely the last click — it warms up customers who then convert through paid search. Switch to multi-touch attribution and email gets a very different story.
new example: Multi-touch attribution shows that email also helped.

old definition: The true additional lift a marketing activity generates — above and beyond what would have happened without it. High ROAS does not always mean high incrementality: some of your spend captures customers who would have bought anyway.
new definition: The extra sales that only happen because of an ad.
old example: Riley said: Our retargeting campaigns have a 12x ROAS. But if we look at incrementality — the sales that only happened because of the retargeting — it is closer to 2x. We are spending a lot of money to show ads to people who were going to buy regardless. That is wasted budget.
new example: The incrementality test showed the ads added 10% more sales.

old definition: The average cost to acquire one new customer across all channels combined. Blended CAC gives a realistic picture of overall acquisition efficiency — unlike channel-level CAC, which can look strong while the total is unsustainable.
new definition: The average cost to win one customer across all channels.
old example: Riley said: Your paid search CAC looks excellent at £30. But your blended CAC — including the brand spend, the content team, and the agency fees — is £180. The board needs to understand the blended number, not the best-performing channel in isolation.
new example: Our blended CAC is £40 per customer.

old definition: Return On Ad Spend — the revenue generated for every pound spent on advertising. A ROAS of 4x means every £1 spent on ads generates £4 in revenue. It measures efficiency but not profitability.
new definition: Short for return on ad spend: money earned for every pound spent on ads.
old example: Riley said: ROAS is a useful metric but not the whole story. A 10x ROAS sounds great — until you factor in your cost of goods, fulfilment, and customer service costs. A channel with a 5x ROAS and low overheads can be more profitable than one with 10x and high fulfilment costs.
new example: Our ROAS is four, so we earn £4 for every £1.

old definition: The time it takes for a customer to generate enough revenue to cover the cost of acquiring them. A short payback period means the business recoups its acquisition cost quickly and can reinvest in more growth.
new definition: How long it takes to earn back the cost of a new customer.
old example: Riley said: Our blended CAC is £150 and our average monthly revenue per customer is £30. That is a five-month payback period. The business can afford that if customers stay for two years. If they churn at six months, we barely break even — and we cannot fund growth.
new example: Our payback period is six months.

old definition: A statistical method that uses historical data to measure how different marketing channels contribute to overall business outcomes. It is particularly useful for channels that are difficult to track at the individual level, like TV, radio, and out-of-home.
new definition: Using past data to see how each channel affects sales.
old example: Riley said: We cannot track TV at the individual conversion level — but we can see that markets where we ran TV consistently perform 15% better across all digital metrics. That is media mix modelling at work: using aggregate data to understand a channel's contribution.
new example: Media mix modelling showed that TV still works for us.

old definition: A measurement approach that tracks performance across every stage of the customer journey — from awareness to conversion to retention — rather than just measuring the bottom of the funnel.
new definition: Measuring results at every step of the customer journey.
old example: Riley said: Bottom-funnel ROAS looks brilliant because you are measuring the stage where people are already close to buying. Full-funnel measurement shows you what filled the top — and whether your brand and awareness investment is actually driving long-term performance or whether you are just harvesting existing demand.
new example: Full-funnel measurement tracks views, clicks and sales.

word: What is our blended CAC this quarter?
old definition: A key performance question that asks for the total average cost of customer acquisition across all channels — not just the best-performing one. It gives a realistic picture of acquisition efficiency.
new definition: A question about the average cost of getting a customer.
old example: Riley opened the performance review: Before we look at individual channel ROAS, let me ask: what is our blended CAC this quarter? I want to see the real cost — all channel spend, agency fees, content production — divided by net new customers. That is the number we optimise.
new example: Before we spend more, what is our blended CAC this quarter?

word: We need to run an incrementality test
old definition: A signal that the team needs to measure whether a marketing activity is generating genuine new demand — or just capturing people who were already going to convert. Incrementality tests typically involve holding out a group from seeing the campaign.
new definition: A way to say we must check if ads really bring extra sales.
old example: Riley said: Retargeting is showing a 15x ROAS but I do not believe it. We need to run an incrementality test — hold back 20% of the retargeting audience and see if they still convert. If the conversion rate is similar with no retargeting, we are not generating lift — we are spending to take credit.
new example: We need to run an incrementality test on our search ads.

word: The attribution model is distorting the picture
old definition: A phrase used to flag that the current way of assigning credit to marketing channels is creating a misleading view of performance — causing the team to over-invest in some channels and under-invest in others.
new definition: A warning that the credit system gives the wrong idea.
old example: Riley said: The attribution model is distorting the picture. We are optimising for last-click performance, so paid search looks like a hero and everything upstream — display, social, email — looks like it is doing nothing. Switch to multi-touch and the whole story changes.
new example: The attribution model is distorting the picture, so social media looks weak.

word: ROAS does not tell us if we are profitable
old definition: A reminder that ROAS measures revenue efficiency but not profitability — it does not account for cost of goods sold, fulfilment, customer service, or returns. High ROAS can coexist with unprofitability.
new definition: A reminder that high ad returns don't always mean profit.
old example: The junior analyst presented a 12x ROAS and called it a success. Riley said: ROAS does not tell us if we are profitable. I need to see the contribution margin after cost of goods and fulfilment. A 12x ROAS on a 10% margin product might be generating less profit than a 4x ROAS on a 60% margin one.
new example: ROAS does not tell us if we are profitable, so check the costs too.

word: Let's look at this through a full-funnel lens
old definition: A phrase that redirects analysis from bottom-of-funnel metrics only to a view that includes awareness, consideration, and retention stages. It prevents over-optimisation for short-term conversion at the expense of long-term growth.
new definition: A suggestion to look at every step, not just sales.
old example: Marcus said: Organic traffic is down but conversion rate is up — is that a problem? Riley said: Let's look at this through a full-funnel lens. If top-of-funnel traffic is declining, conversion rate can look good for a few months while the pipeline quietly dries up. We are probably harvesting existing demand, not building new.
new example: Let's look at this through a full-funnel lens before we cut the budget.

word: What is the payback period at current CAC?
old definition: A key financial question that connects acquisition cost to revenue and retention — asking how long the business must retain a customer before it recoups what it spent to acquire them.
new definition: A question about how long it takes to earn back the cost of a customer.
old example: Riley said: Before we increase the acquisition budget, I want to know: what is the payback period at current CAC? If we are spending £200 to acquire a customer who pays us £40 a month, that is a five-month payback — which is sustainable only if we retain for at least 12 months. What does our cohort data say?
new example: What is the payback period at current CAC? Is it under a year?

old definition: A self-reinforcing growth loop in which a community gets more valuable as more people join — and that value attracts more members. Once a flywheel is spinning, it becomes increasingly difficult for competitors to replicate.
new definition: When a community grows and gets better because members bring new members.
old example: Riley explained: The community flywheel works like this. More members create more content and conversations. More content attracts new members. New members contribute more content. At a certain point, the community grows itself — you are not pushing the flywheel, it is pulling you.
new example: Our community flywheel keeps bringing in new users.

old definition: A customer or community member who actively promotes the brand — through content, referrals, events, or advocacy. Unlike influencers, ambassadors are usually long-term, deeply engaged, and motivated by genuine belief in the brand rather than payment alone.
new definition: A customer who happily promotes a brand.
old example: Riley said: Our brand ambassadors are not paid to post — they post because they genuinely believe in what we are building. They answer questions in our community, share our content with their networks, and help onboard new members. That kind of advocacy is worth more than any paid campaign.
new example: Each ambassador shares our product with friends.

old definition: Involving community members in creating products, content, or campaigns — rather than just consuming them. Co-creation builds deep ownership and loyalty, and often produces better ideas than an internal team alone.
new definition: Making products or content together with customers.
old example: Marcus said: We launched our new product feature after six months of co-creation with our top 50 community members. Riley said: That is exactly how it should work. Those members became the product's biggest advocates at launch — because they helped build it. Co-creation turns customers into stakeholders.
new example: The new flavour came from co-creation with our fans.

old definition: An online space where community members can discuss topics, ask questions, and share knowledge. A well-managed forum is one of the highest-value assets a brand community can have — it creates content, builds SEO, and reduces support costs.
new definition: A website where people discuss topics.
old example: Riley said: Our forum generates 40,000 organic search visits per month and reduces customer support tickets by 30%. Members answer each other's questions. The brand is the facilitator — not the provider of every answer. That is a community asset that a campaign can never replicate.
new example: Users help each other on our forum.

old definition: User-Generated Content strategy — a plan for encouraging, curating, and amplifying content created by customers and community members. UGC is typically more trusted than branded content and cheaper to produce.
new definition: A plan to get customers to make content about your brand.
old example: Riley said: Our UGC strategy is simple — make it easy for customers to share, amplify the best content through our channels, and give creators visibility and recognition. We get authentic content for free. They get an audience. That is a fair exchange and it builds community at the same time.
new example: Our UGC strategy asks fans to share photos with our hashtag.

old definition: A measure of how active, engaged, and positive a community is. Community health metrics include active member rates, content contribution rates, sentiment, and the ratio of passive to active members.
new definition: How active and positive a community is.
old example: Riley opened the community review: Let's talk about community health before we talk about size. We have 50,000 members but only 3% are active contributors. That is a passive audience, not a community. A healthy community has a much higher participation rate and a strong culture of mutual support.
new example: Community health is good: people post every day.

old definition: A cycle in which satisfied customers share their experience, attract new customers, who then become satisfied and share in turn. A strong advocacy loop reduces dependence on paid acquisition.
new definition: When happy customers bring new customers, who then do the same.
old example: Riley said: If we can get 10% of our customers to actively refer one new customer each, our advocacy loop reduces paid CAC by 30%. That is not a rounding error — that is a structural shift in how the business grows. Build the loop, measure it, and optimise it like any other channel.
new example: Reviews and referrals create a strong advocacy loop.

old definition: The percentage of community members who actively participate — posting, replying, reacting, or contributing — in a given period. Engagement rate is a better measure of community quality than total member count.
new definition: The percentage of people who like, comment or share.
old example: Marcus said: We have 100,000 forum members. Riley said: What is the engagement rate? If 2% are active, you have 2,000 engaged people and 98,000 dormant accounts. Size means very little — engagement rate is what tells you whether the community is alive or just collecting sign-ups.
new example: Our engagement rate is 8% this month.

old definition: A strategic framing that positions the brand community itself — not the marketing around it — as the primary value driver. It signals that community is not a channel but an asset that compounds over time.
new definition: A way to say people join for the community, not just the product.
old example: Riley said at the strategy session: I want to reframe how we think about this. The community is the product. It is not a marketing channel — it is the thing that makes our product stickier, our retention stronger, and our advocacy cheaper. We should resource it like a product, not a campaign.
new example: For our app, the community is the product.

old definition: A community management question that identifies the most active, influential members — typically the candidates for ambassador programmes and co-creation projects.
new definition: A question about the most active members.
old example: Riley asked the community team: Who are our top contributors? I want to know the 1% who answer the most questions, create the most content, and bring in the most new members. Those are the people we need to invest in — recognition, early access, co-creation opportunities. That is how a flywheel starts.
new example: Who are our top contributors? Let's thank them.

word: We are harvesting the community, not growing it
old definition: A critical observation that signals a community is being used for short-term marketing purposes — promotions, campaigns, announcements — without giving enough back to members. Harvesting kills community health over time.
new definition: A warning that you take from a community but give nothing back.
old example: Riley reviewed the community activity log: All of our posts are brand announcements and product promotions. We are harvesting the community, not growing it. Members join for connection and value — not to be sold to. We need to give significantly more than we take.
new example: Too many sales posts. We are harvesting the community, not growing it.

old definition: A call to action to design a deliberate process through which satisfied customers share their experience and attract new ones. It treats advocacy as a growth channel to be built, measured, and optimised — not a happy accident.
new definition: A way to say create a system where happy customers bring others.
old example: Riley said: Word of mouth is already happening — customers are sharing their experience on social and in forums. But it is unstructured. Let's build the advocacy loop deliberately: make it easy to share, reward the best advocates, and measure referral as a primary acquisition channel.
new example: Build the advocacy loop with a simple referral reward.

word: What does the community health look like?
old definition: A diagnostic question about the quality and vitality of a community — asking about active participation rates, sentiment, and the balance of contribution versus passive consumption.
new definition: A question about how active and happy members are.
old example: Before investing more in community growth, Riley asked: What does the community health look like? We have 80,000 members but if engagement rate is below 5%, we do not have a community — we have a mailing list. Show me the active contributor rate, the content creation trend, and the sentiment scores.
new example: Before the launch, what does the community health look like?

old definition: The foundational principle of community-led marketing — brands that contribute value to a community earn the right to ask for something in return. Brands that only ask (promote, sell, announce) are extracting from a community, not building one.
new definition: A rule to help people first, then ask for something.
old example: Riley said: Before we ask the community to share our campaign, we need to give before we ask. What have we given this community in the last 30 days? Resources, recognition, access, support? The ratio should be ten to one — ten acts of generosity for every one ask. If we are not there, the ask will fall flat.
new example: Give before you ask: share free tips before you sell.

old definition: A type of artificial intelligence that creates new content — text, images, audio, or video — based on patterns it has learned from large amounts of existing data. In marketing, generative AI is used to write copy, create images, draft emails, and produce first versions of content at scale.
new definition: AI that creates new text, images or video.
old example: Generative AI produced the first three drafts of the campaign copy in under a minute. The team used those drafts as a starting point and refined them with brand-specific language. What used to take two days now takes two hours.
new example: We use generative AI to write first drafts of posts.

old definition: A type of AI system trained on enormous amounts of text that can understand and generate human language. The technology behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude. In marketing, large language models power chatbots, copy generators, and search tools. Often abbreviated as LLM.
new definition: An AI system trained on lots of text that can write like a person.
old example: The LLM powering Forge's screening tool reads every application and ranks candidates by fit before a recruiter opens a single CV. The model was trained on millions of examples of successful placements in similar roles. The team treats its output as a starting recommendation, not a final decision.
new example: A large language model wrote these product descriptions.

old definition: Using data and AI to predict what a specific customer will want to see or buy next — and showing them that, rather than generic content. Predictive personalisation makes the customer experience feel relevant and tailored without requiring manual segmentation for each individual.
new definition: Using AI to guess what each customer wants to see.
old example: Kova's email system uses predictive personalisation to decide which product to feature in each customer's weekly digest. It learns from past clicks and purchase history to anticipate what each person is most likely to act on. Open rates improved by 34% in the first month.
new example: Predictive personalisation shows each user different products.

old definition: Content that changes automatically based on who is viewing it — their location, behaviour, purchase history, or stage in the customer journey. A dynamic email shows different images, offers, or text to different people based on their data. Dynamic content is how personalisation happens at scale.
new definition: Content that changes for each person who sees it.
old example: The same landing page shows different headlines, images, and offers to each visitor based on their industry and company size. Flux built its entire campaign architecture around dynamic content so no two prospect segments see the same message. Conversion rates improved significantly once the generic version was retired.
new example: Our emails use dynamic content, so each one shows the reader's name.

old definition: The skill of writing clear, specific instructions — called prompts — that get an AI tool to produce the output you actually want. Good prompt engineering is a practical skill for anyone using generative AI in marketing. The quality of the AI output is often directly determined by the quality of the prompt.
new definition: Writing clear instructions to get good results from AI.
old example: A vague prompt produces generic output; a precise prompt with context, format, and constraints produces something usable. The marketing team spent two days developing prompt templates before launching the AI drafting workflow. Prompt engineering turned out to be the most valuable skill for getting consistent results from the model.
new example: Good prompt engineering gives us better headlines.

old definition: The tendency to trust and follow AI or automated system outputs without critically checking them — even when they are wrong. Automation bias is a real risk in marketing teams that use AI heavily. It happens when people stop reviewing AI outputs carefully because the technology feels reliable.
new definition: Trusting a computer's answer too much without checking it.
old example: The team published a statistic from an AI-generated report without checking the original source. When the client asked for the citation, the number turned out not to exist. That incident became the founding case for Forge's policy requiring human verification of every AI-generated claim.
new example: Automation bias made us miss a wrong price in the ad.

old definition: The set of rules, processes, and standards an organisation uses to make sure its AI tools are used responsibly, ethically, and in line with legal requirements. In marketing, AI governance covers things like data privacy, content approval, bias checking, and transparency with customers about when AI has been used.
new definition: Rules for using AI safely and fairly.
old example: Forge's AI governance framework defines who can use which tools, for what purpose, and how outputs must be reviewed before publication. Without it, teams were making inconsistent decisions about when to trust AI output and when to check it. The framework reduced errors significantly in the first quarter after launch.
new example: Our AI governance says a person checks every ad.

old definition: Using technology to complete a series of marketing tasks automatically — without a person having to trigger each step manually. Workflow automation connects tools and systems so that when one thing happens, the next thing happens automatically. Common in email sequences, lead nurturing, social scheduling, and reporting.
new definition: Using software to do tasks automatically.
old example: Workflow automation replaced a manual four-step reporting process with a single scheduled script. The weekly performance report now arrives automatically every Monday morning without anyone building it by hand. It saved approximately six hours per week across the marketing function.
new example: Workflow automation sends a welcome email to every new user.

word: THE AI IS HALLUCINATING — IT HAS...
old definition: A phrase used to explain that an AI tool has produced content that sounds confident and plausible but is factually wrong. AI hallucination is a real technical limitation — the model generates text based on patterns, not on verified facts, and sometimes produces errors with complete fluency.
new definition: A way to say the AI has made up false information.
old example: The AI is hallucinating — the statistic it cited in paragraph three does not appear in any of the source documents. Riley flagged it in the review and Dana confirmed the figure was fabricated. Every AI-generated claim now goes to fact-check before anything reaches the client.
new example: The AI is hallucinating; it has invented a customer quote.

word: WE NEED A HUMAN IN THE LOOP FOR...
old definition: A phrase for identifying tasks where AI output must be reviewed, approved, or corrected by a person before it is used. Human-in-the-loop processes exist to catch AI errors, ensure brand alignment, manage legal risk, and maintain quality. Used in AI governance discussions and content workflow planning.
new definition: A way to say a person must check the AI's work.
old example: We need a human in the loop for any content that makes a product claim or cites a specific number. The AI can draft it efficiently, but it cannot verify that the claim is accurate. Sign-off sits with the content lead before anything goes live.
new example: We need a human in the loop for all legal text.

word: THE PROMPT NEEDS TO BE MORE SPECIFIC ABOUT...
old definition: A phrase for giving feedback on an AI prompt that is too vague and producing poor or generic output. Used in team reviews of AI workflows to improve the quality of AI outputs by improving the instructions given to the model.
new definition: A way to say the AI instructions are too vague.
old example: The prompt needs to be more specific about the audience — the output reads as generic B2C when we need enterprise B2B tone. Marcus rewrote it with a persona, a word count, and three formatting constraints. The second version was usable without further editing.
new example: The prompt needs to be more specific about the audience.

word: WE ARE USING AI TO AUGMENT, NOT REPLACE...
old definition: A phrase for clarifying that AI tools are designed to support and enhance human work — not to eliminate human involvement. Used when communicating AI strategy internally to address team concerns, or when explaining the role of AI in a workflow to stakeholders.
new definition: A way to say AI helps people but doesn't take their jobs.
old example: We are using AI to augment, not replace, the copywriting team. The writers use AI to handle first drafts at volume and focus their creative energy on the ideas and the refinement. Output has tripled without adding headcount.
new example: We are using AI to augment, not replace, our writers.

word: OUR AI GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK REQUIRES THAT...
old definition: A phrase for explaining a specific rule or requirement within an organisation's AI usage policy. Used when briefing teams on AI guidelines, reviewing content workflows, or explaining to clients how the organisation manages AI risk.
new definition: A way to explain a rule about using AI.
old example: Our AI governance framework requires that every piece of AI-generated copy is reviewed by a human editor before it goes live. Dana updated the workflow documentation to reflect the new approval step. The framework applies to all channels, including social and paid.
new example: Our AI governance framework requires that a person approves every post.

word: THE OUTPUT NEEDS A HUMAN EDIT BEFORE...
old definition: A phrase for flagging that an AI-generated piece of content is not ready to use and needs human revision before it can be published, shared, or sent. Used in content review meetings and workflow sign-off processes to maintain quality and brand standards.
new definition: A way to say AI text must be checked by a person first.
old example: The output needs a human edit before it goes to the client — the draft is strong but three phrases feel off-brand. Riley corrected them in under ten minutes. The client never saw the raw version, which is exactly how the workflow is designed to function.
new example: The output needs a human edit before we publish it.

old definition: A written statement that an organisation sends to journalists and media outlets to share official news — a product launch, a new appointment, a financial result, or a major announcement. A good press release tells the journalist the story clearly and quickly, and includes everything they need to write about it.
new definition: A written news story a company sends to journalists.
old example: Forge issued a press release announcing the acquisition at 7 AM when the market opened. The document had been written, approved, and embargoed two weeks in advance. Three major trade publications had it live within the hour.
new example: We sent a press release about our new store.

old definition: An agreement between an organisation and a journalist that the journalist receives information early — but cannot publish it until a specific date and time. Embargoes give journalists time to prepare a story in advance. Breaking an embargo — publishing before the agreed time — is a serious breach of trust in the media industry.
new definition: An agreement that a journalist won't publish news until a set time.
old example: The results went to financial press under embargo at 6 AM with a publication time of 7 AM. Every outlet honoured it. The one that had broken an embargo the previous year was not on the distribution list.
new example: The embargo ends at 9am on Monday.

old definition: A collection of resources that an organisation gives to journalists to help them cover a story. A media kit typically includes a press release, high-resolution images, key facts and statistics, executive biographies, and background information about the company or product. The goal is to give journalists everything they need in one place.
new definition: A pack of photos and facts for journalists.
old example: Kova's media kit contains the brand assets, key executive biographies, the latest press releases, and the company fact sheet. When a journalist picks up the story, everything they need is in one place. It is updated quarterly.
new example: The media kit has our logo, photos and key facts.

old definition: The person who officially represents an organisation and communicates on its behalf with the media, the public, or other external audiences. A spokesperson needs to be briefed on key messages, trained to handle difficult questions, and authorised to speak on the topics they are covering.
new definition: The person who speaks to the media for a company.
old example: The spokesperson was briefed on every anticipated question before the press conference. She knew which topics were on the record, which were background, and which she would not comment on. Her preparation showed — she handled the regulatory question without hesitation.
new example: Our spokesperson will answer questions on TV.

old definition: Information shared with a journalist that they agree not to attribute to you or publish directly. Going off the record is a way of giving a journalist background context or a candid view without having it reported as an official statement. However, off the record only works if the journalist agrees to it — and it should be agreed before the information is shared, not after.
new definition: Information a journalist agrees not to publish with your name.
old example: Dana shared the background context off the record before the journalist filed the story. The information shaped the framing without appearing in the article. Used correctly, off the record is a tool for accuracy, not concealment.
new example: She told the reporter the news off the record.

old definition: A meeting or call between an organisation's representative and a journalist — usually to share news, provide background information, or give the journalist access to a key person before a story is published. A media briefing is more targeted than a press conference and more personal than a press release.
new definition: A meeting where a company gives news to journalists.
old example: Forge held a media briefing for six financial journalists the day before the earnings announcement. The session was background only — no recording, no direct quotes. It gave journalists the context to write informed stories the moment the release went public.
new example: The media briefing starts at ten o'clock.

old definition: The specific element of a story that makes it timely, interesting, or relevant enough for a journalist to want to cover it right now. Without a news hook, a story has no reason to be published today rather than any other day. A strong news hook connects your announcement to something already in the news, a current trend, or a specific moment in time.
new definition: The part of a story that makes it new and interesting.
