new definition: A way to say something looks good but has hidden problems.
old example: 'On the surface, the revenue numbers look strong. But on closer inspection, 60% of that revenue comes from three customers — any one of which could leave.'
new example: On the surface, sales look strong, but on closer inspection, most come from one client.

word: THE KEY RISK WE IDENTIFIED IS...
old definition: A phrase used to name the single most important danger found during the due diligence process.
new definition: A way to name the biggest danger you found.
old example: 'The key risk we identified is over-reliance on a single product line. If consumer preferences shift — and they are already showing signs of doing so — the business is very exposed.'
new example: The key risk we identified is their old technology.

word: THIS IS NOT REFLECTED IN THE CURRENT VALUATION
old definition: A phrase used when the price being asked does not account for a problem or risk found during due diligence.
new definition: A way to say the price ignores a problem.
old example: Riley said: The NPS has dropped from +38 to +12 in 18 months. That represents a significant deterioration in customer loyalty — and this is not reflected in the current valuation.
new example: Their brand is weak, and this is not reflected in the current valuation.

old definition: A phrase used to highlight the value that cannot easily be put on a balance sheet — brand reputation, community, loyalty.
new definition: A way to describe value you can't easily measure.
old example: 'The intangibles here are significant. The brand has a 20-year heritage and a loyal community of advocates. That takes years to build and cannot simply be bought or replicated.'
new example: The intangibles here are a loyal community and a famous name.

word: OUR RECOMMENDATION IS TO [PROCEED / NOT PROCEED] BECAUSE...
old definition: The standard closing phrase of a due diligence report — a clear verdict followed by the main reason.
new definition: A way to give a final yes or no with a reason.
old example: 'Our recommendation is to proceed, but with a renegotiated valuation. The brand has genuine value — but the loyalty data suggests the current price is approximately 20% too high.'
new example: Our recommendation is to proceed because the brand is very strong.

old definition: The study of signs and symbols — how they create meaning. In marketing, it helps explain why a logo or colour makes people feel a certain way.
new definition: The study of signs and symbols and what they mean.
old example: Riley said: Semiotics is why a red logo feels urgent and a blue one feels trustworthy. It's not accidental — it's a system of meaning built over time.
new example: Semiotics helps us understand why red means danger.

old definition: The physical thing you see or hear — the image, word, or sound itself.
new definition: The thing you see or hear, like a picture or word.
old example: The golden arches are the signifier. They're just two yellow curves. But they immediately trigger a meaning in the viewer's mind.
new example: The apple in the logo is the signifier.

old definition: The concept or meaning that the signifier creates in your mind.
new definition: The idea that a sign makes you think of.
old example: The signifier is the apple with a bite taken out. The signified is creativity, simplicity, and premium quality — everything Apple wants you to feel.
new example: The signified is health and freshness.

old definition: The emotional or cultural meaning attached to something — beyond its literal description.
new definition: The feeling or idea something suggests.
old example: White has the connotation of purity and simplicity in Western markets. In some Asian markets, the connotation is mourning. Brand teams miss this all the time.
new example: Gold has a connotation of luxury.

old definition: The literal, factual meaning of something — what it actually is, with no added meaning.
new definition: The basic, literal meaning of something.
old example: The denotation of a dove is 'a bird'. The connotation is peace and purity. Dove soap used the connotation — not the denotation — to build its brand.
new example: The denotation of the image is just a dog on a beach.

old definition: The complete set of visual elements that represent a brand — logo, colours, typography, and imagery.
new definition: All the visual parts of a brand, like logo and colours.
old example: Riley said: The visual identity tells customers who you are before they read a single word. If it looks cheap, they assume the product is cheap.
new example: Our visual identity uses blue and white.

old definition: The symbols and images that a brand uses consistently — and what those images communicate.
new definition: The symbols and images a brand uses again and again.
old example: Marcus said: Their iconography is all straight lines and sharp angles. Riley said: Which signals precision, efficiency, and no-nonsense — exactly right for a B2B tech brand.
new example: The brand's iconography includes stars and waves.

old definition: The visual equivalent of tone — how formal, playful, minimal, or bold a brand\'s visual style is.
new definition: How formal or playful a design looks.
old example: The new packaging has the wrong visual register. It looks fun and casual — but the product is a premium medical device. The design is sending the wrong message.
new example: The visual register is calm and simple.

old definition: A phrase used to describe what something literally shows before moving on to what it means.
new definition: A way to describe what something literally shows.
old example: 'At the denotative level, this logo is simply a circle and a line. But at the connotative level, it signals completeness, unity, and a global reach.'
new example: At the denotative level, the ad shows a woman drinking tea.

old definition: A phrase used to describe the overall style and what it communicates — treating design as a form of communication.
new definition: A way to describe the style of a design.
old example: Riley said: The visual language here is minimal and cold — clean white backgrounds, no warmth, very clinical. That works for a laboratory. It does not work for a food brand.
new example: The visual language here is clean and modern.

word: THIS COMMUNICATES [QUALITY] TO THE VIEWER BECAUSE...
old definition: A phrase used when explaining the effect of a specific visual choice on the audience.
new definition: A way to explain the effect of a design choice.
old example: 'The serif typeface communicates authority and tradition to the viewer because serif fonts have historical associations with print, academia, and longevity.'
new example: This communicates trust to the viewer because the colours are calm.

old definition: A direct phrase for naming what a specific visual element implies — beyond its literal meaning.
new definition: A way to say what a visual detail suggests.
old example: 'The connotation of the dark navy blue is stability and trustworthiness. Combined with gold, it signals premium and exclusive — which is the right positioning for this client.'
new example: The connotation of the green leaf is nature.

word: THERE IS A TENSION BETWEEN [X] AND [Y] IN THIS IDENTITY
old definition: A phrase used in a critique when two elements of a visual identity are sending conflicting messages.
new definition: A way to say two parts of a design send different messages.
old example: Riley said: There is a tension between the playful illustration style and the formal corporate typeface in this identity. They are fighting each other rather than working together.
new example: There is a tension between luxury and low price in this identity.

old definition: A closing phrase in a visual critique that summarises what the identity communicates as a whole.
new definition: A way to sum up how a design feels.
old example: 'The overall effect is one of energy and disruption — which is perfect for a challenger brand. But it may alienate the more traditional buyers in their current client base.'
new example: The overall effect is fresh and friendly.

old definition: Using as few words as possible while still being clear. In executive writing, brevity is a sign of respect for the reader\'s time.
new definition: Using few words while staying clear.
old example: Riley said: The CEO doesn't want three paragraphs. She wants three bullets. Brevity isn't laziness — it's one of the hardest skills in business writing.
new example: Brevity matters, so keep your email to five lines.

old definition: Using exactly the right word to express exactly the right meaning — no more, no less.
new definition: Using exactly the right words.
old example: Marcus said: Instead of 'we are looking to possibly improve revenue performance going forward', write 'we will increase revenue by 15% in Q3'. That's precision.
new example: Precision helps busy leaders understand you quickly.

old definition: A conclusion the reader reaches themselves based on the information you give them — without you saying it directly.
new definition: A conclusion the reader reaches from the facts.
old example: The memo said costs are up 22% and revenue is flat. The inference the board drew was obvious: the business model is under pressure. I didn't need to write that line.
new example: The obvious inference is that we need a bigger budget.

old definition: Something you suggest or indicate without saying it openly. Often used in formal writing to soften a direct statement.
new definition: A meaning that is suggested, not said directly.
old example: The implication of the report was that the current team lacks the skills needed for the next phase. Riley chose not to say that directly — but every executive in the room understood it.
new example: The implication of the report is that we must act now.

old definition: The quality of writing that makes the reader trust you — a confident tone, clear structure, and no unnecessary hedging.
new definition: Writing that sounds confident and trustworthy.
old example: Marcus said: The draft keeps using phrases like 'it might be worth considering' and 'perhaps we could'. That language has no authority. Write 'I recommend' and 'we should' instead.
new example: Short, clear sentences give your writing authority.

old definition: A short section at the top of a report that gives the key findings and recommendations — so a busy leader can read just that and understand the whole document.
new definition: A short section at the top that gives the main points.
old example: Riley said: Put your most important recommendation first. The executive summary is not an introduction — it\'s the whole story in 150 words. Everything after it is the evidence.
new example: Most directors only read the executive summary.

old definition: A business document written specifically to help someone make a decision — it sets out the options, the recommendation, and the trade-offs clearly.
new definition: A document written to help someone make a choice.
old example: Marcus said: Stop writing reports and start writing decision documents. Every page should answer: what do we need to decide, and what do we recommend? That's what the C-suite needs from us.
new example: The decision document lists three options and their costs.

old definition: Words, sentences, or sections that add length but not meaning. In C-suite writing, noise kills credibility.
new definition: Extra words that add length but not meaning.
old example: I cut 600 words from the proposal and it became three times more persuasive. The noise was masking the argument. Every word that doesn't earn its place is noise.
new example: Cut the noise and keep only the key facts.

old definition: The professional way to open a C-suite communication — state the recommendation first, then the reasoning.
new definition: A clear way to start with what you suggest.
old example: 'The recommendation is to close the Manchester office and consolidate operations in Leeds by Q4. This will reduce fixed costs by £400k annually and improve team efficiency.'
new example: The recommendation is to launch in March.

old definition: A phrase that focuses a document or meeting on what actually needs to be decided — cutting through background and context.
new definition: A way to focus on what must be decided.
old example: 'The key decision here is whether to invest in the platform rebuild now or patch the current system for another 18 months. Both options have significant implications for the roadmap.'
new example: The key decision here is whether to hire a new agency.

old definition: A phrase used to signal that you\'re moving from context to a plain statement — useful in documents where you need to land a hard message clearly.
new definition: A way to say something plainly.
old example: 'To put it directly, the current marketing spend is not producing returns that justify the budget. We recommend a 30% reduction and a reallocation to performance channels.'
new example: To put it directly, the campaign lost money.

word: THE IMPLICATION FOR [THE BUSINESS/THE TEAM] IS...
old definition: A phrase used to make the "so what" explicit — connecting data or analysis to its real business impact.
new definition: A way to explain what a result means for the company.
old example: 'Customer satisfaction scores have dropped 12 points over two quarters. The implication for the business is that churn is likely to increase in H2 unless the service model is changed.'
new example: The implication for the business is lower costs.

old definition: An informal phrase used to signal that you\'re skipping the background and getting straight to the point. Used in spoken executive briefings more than in formal documents.
new definition: An informal way to skip details and say the main point.
old example: Marcus said: I know you've read the background section. Cut to the chase: we need a decision on budget by Friday or we lose the agency retainer.
new example: Cut to the chase: we need more budget.

word: WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE IS...
old definition: A phrase used to translate abstract findings or data into concrete, real-world impact that an executive can act on.
new definition: A way to explain what an idea means in real life.
old example: 'The model shows a 7% drop in conversion. What this means in practice is that we\'re losing approximately 340 sales a month — or £1.2m in annual revenue at current prices.'
new example: What this means in practice is two more people in the team.

old definition: A measure of how much advertising exposure a campaign delivers. One GRP = 1% of the target audience reached once. 200 GRPs = 100% reached twice, or 50% reached four times.
new definition: A measure of how many people see an advert and how often.
old example: Riley said: The plan delivers 350 GRPs over six weeks. That's a decent weight for a brand awareness campaign in a new market. But we need to check the reach and frequency split.
new example: The campaign delivered 300 GRPs in Spain.

old definition: The cost of reaching 1,000 people with an ad. A standard metric for comparing how efficient different media channels or placements are.
new definition: The cost of showing an advert to 1,000 people.
old example: Marcus said: The CPT for TV in Germany is €18. Online video is €6. Riley said: Don't just buy the cheapest CPT — check whether the quality of the audience exposure is comparable.
new example: The CPT for online video is lower than for TV.

old definition: The total volume of advertising activity in a market — usually measured in GRPs or spend. A heavier media weight means more exposure.
new definition: The total amount of advertising in a market.
old example: We're outspent three to one in France. Until we match the competitor's media weight, we can't expect to shift brand awareness metrics. You can't whisper in a shouting match.
new example: We need more media weight in Germany.

old definition: A media scheduling strategy where advertising runs in planned bursts (flights) with gaps in between, rather than continuously.
new definition: Running adverts in short bursts with breaks in between.
old example: Riley said: The budget doesn't cover 52 weeks of activity. So we're flighting — four weeks on, four weeks off, across the whole year. The goal is to maintain presence without spreading the budget too thin.
new example: Flighting helps us save money in quiet months.

old definition: Your brand\'s advertising spend as a percentage of all advertising spend in the category. If the total market spends £10m and you spend £2m, your SOV is 20%.
new definition: Your share of all the advertising in your market.
old example: Marcus said: Our share of voice has dropped from 35% to 22% since the competitor increased their spend. Riley said: Then we're buying market share decline. SOV below share of market means we'll lose ground.
new example: Our share of voice is 20% in France.

old definition: When your share of voice equals your share of market — the breakeven point. Above parity typically means market share growth; below means decline.
new definition: When your share of advertising matches your share of sales.
old example: The goal for the first year is SOV parity — match the competitor's presence so we at least stop losing ground. In year two, we go above parity to grow.
new example: We are at SOV parity in the UK.

old definition: The number (or percentage) of unique people who see your ad at least once during a campaign. Different from impressions, which count each view.
new definition: The number of different people who see an advert.
old example: Riley said: The plan delivers 75% reach among adults 25-54 in the UK. That means three out of every four people in our target audience will see the campaign at least once.
new example: The TV campaign had a reach of five million people.

old definition: The average number of times each person in your target audience sees your ad during a campaign.
new definition: How many times each person sees an advert.
old example: Marcus said: We have great reach but the frequency is only 1.8. Riley said: For a new brand message, we need a minimum of three to four. People don't remember an ad they've only seen twice.
new example: A frequency of three is enough for this campaign.

old definition: The standard phrase for describing what a media plan will achieve in terms of exposure for a specific target group.
new definition: A way to say how much exposure a plan gives.
old example: 'The plan delivers 280 GRPs against adults 18-34, with a reach of 68% and an average frequency of 4.1 over the eight-week flight.'
new example: The plan delivers 400 GRPs against young adults.

old definition: A phrase used when a competitor\'s media spend is higher than yours in a specific market — meaning your share of voice is lower.
new definition: A way to say a competitor spends more than you.
old example: 'We're outspent in Italy by a ratio of two to one. Until we address that imbalance, it's very difficult to build brand awareness against a competitor with double our media weight.'
new example: We're outspent in Italy, so our ads are less visible.

old definition: A phrase used to describe a period of concentrated advertising activity within a flighted media schedule.
new definition: A way to say how long a burst of adverts lasts.
old example: 'We're running a six-week flight in Q3, then going dark in Q4 to save budget for the January relaunch. The GRP weight during the flight is 300 — enough to build meaningful reach.'
new example: We're running a four-week flight in September.

word: THE CPT IS [X] — COMPARED TO [Y] FOR [CHANNEL]
old definition: A phrase used when comparing the cost efficiency of different channels or placements.
new definition: A way to compare costs between channels.
old example: 'The CPT for premium TV spots is €22. Compared to €7 for pre-roll video. The TV reach is broader but the digital targeting is more precise — which matters for this campaign.'
new example: The CPT is £5 — compared to £12 for TV.

word: OUR SOV IS BELOW / AT / ABOVE PARITY
old definition: A phrase used to describe whether your advertising presence is weaker than, equal to, or stronger than your current market position.
new definition: A way to say if your advertising share matches your sales share.
old example: Riley said: Our SOV is below parity in three of the five markets. That means we're losing ground, even if sales data doesn't show it yet. The brand metrics will follow in six to nine months.
new example: Our SOV is below parity, so we need to spend more.

word: WE NEED TO BALANCE REACH AND FREQUENCY
old definition: A phrase used when discussing how to allocate a media budget — more reach means more unique people, more frequency means showing the ad to the same people more often.
new definition: A way to say you need many viewers and enough repeats.
old example: Marcus said: We need to balance reach and frequency. At the current budget, if we chase 80% reach, frequency drops to 1.5 — which probably isn't enough for message recall. Riley said: Let's model both scenarios.
new example: We need to balance reach and frequency with this small budget.

old definition: The UK\'s independent body that sets and enforces rules about advertising content. The ASA investigates complaints and can require brands to remove or change ads.
new definition: The UK group that checks adverts are honest.
old example: The campaign was referred to the ASA after three consumer complaints. Riley said: The ASA ruled in our favour — the claim was substantiated and the ad didn't mislead. But it was a close call.
new example: The ASA banned the advert last week.

old definition: The UK body that regulates financial services and approves financial promotions. Any marketing for financial products must be FCA-approved before it can run.
new definition: The UK group that controls financial services and their adverts.
old example: Marcus said: Can we use the phrase 'guaranteed returns' in the ad? Riley said: Absolutely not — the FCA prohibits any claim that implies investment returns are guaranteed. We need legal to review every line.
new example: Our bank adverts need FCA approval.

old definition: EU law that controls how organisations collect, store, and use personal data. Marketing teams must comply with GDPR when collecting customer data or sending emails.
new definition: EU law about how companies use personal data.
old example: We can't send that email list to the US agency without a data transfer agreement in place. GDPR doesn't stop at the EU border — the recipient's data handling standards must also be compliant.
new example: Under GDPR, we need permission to send emails.

old definition: A statement added to marketing content to limit claims, clarify conditions, or protect the brand from legal liability.
new definition: A short note that limits or explains a claim.
old example: The headline says 'lose 10kg in 30 days' — that needs a disclaimer immediately below it: 'Results may vary. This claim is based on a clinical study with specific dietary conditions.' Without that, we're in trouble with the ASA.
new example: The disclaimer says 'results may vary'.

old definition: Any statement in advertising that creates a false impression — even if technically true. Regulators assess impact on the average consumer, not the literal meaning of words.
new definition: A statement that gives a false idea.
old example: The phrase '90% of users saw results' is a misleading claim if we don't say the study had only 20 participants. The statistic is true but the impression it creates is false. That's all the regulator needs.
new example: 'Best in the world' could be a misleading claim.

old definition: The evidence that proves a claim in an ad is true. Regulators require that all factual claims can be substantiated before the ad runs.
new definition: Proof that a claim is true.
old example: If you say 'the number one rated product in the category', you need substantiation — a credible, recent source that confirms that rating. If we get an ASA complaint and we can't produce the evidence, the ad comes down.
new example: We need substantiation for the '50% faster' claim.

old definition: A check of marketing content against legal, regulatory, and company policy requirements — usually done by the legal or compliance team before anything is published.
new definition: A check that content follows the rules.
old example: Every piece of marketing copy goes through a compliance review before it goes live. It's not optional — it's part of the process. Riley said: Send the draft to legal by Tuesday. Compliance review takes three working days minimum.
new example: Every advert goes through a compliance review.

old definition: Formal written approval from the legal team that a piece of content is compliant and can be published.
new definition: Official approval from the legal team.
old example: Marcus said: Can we run the campaign tomorrow? Riley said: Not until we have legal sign-off. The financial promotion went to the FCA team this morning — we need their approval in writing before anything goes live.
new example: We are waiting for legal sign-off on the new advert.

old definition: A phrase used during a compliance review to flag that a statement in the copy requires supporting evidence before it can be approved.
new definition: A way to say you need proof for a statement.
old example: 'This claim needs substantiation. You've written that the product is clinically proven — we need the clinical trial data, the publication, and confirmation that it meets the ASA's evidence standard for that claim type.'
new example: 'Number one choice' — this claim needs substantiation.

word: THIS FALLS OUTSIDE WHAT WE CAN SAY
old definition: A phrase used by legal or compliance teams to reject a specific claim or phrase that doesn\'t meet regulatory requirements.
new definition: A way to say a claim is not allowed.
old example: Riley said: 'Best value in the market' — this falls outside what we can say unless we have a credible price comparison study to back it up. Change it to 'competitively priced' or remove it.
new example: Sorry, 'cures headaches' falls outside what we can say.

word: WE NEED LEGAL SIGN-OFF BEFORE THIS GOES LIVE
old definition: A direct reminder that published marketing content must receive formal legal approval — used to stop premature publication.
new definition: A reminder to get legal approval first.
old example: Marcus said: The client wants the campaign live by Friday. Riley said: We need legal sign-off before this goes live. The FCA submission was only made on Monday — three working days minimum. Friday is not realistic.
new example: We need legal sign-off before this goes live on Friday.

old definition: An instruction during copy review to add qualifying text that limits or contextualises a specific claim in the ad.
new definition: An instruction to add a short protective note.
old example: 'Add a disclaimer to cover the weight loss claim — something like: Individual results may vary. This is based on a study conducted under specific dietary and exercise conditions. Without it, the headline is misleading.'
new example: Add a disclaimer to cover the price promise.

word: THIS COULD BE SEEN AS MISLEADING BECAUSE...
old definition: A phrase used to flag copy that might create a false impression — even if it is technically true.
new definition: A way to warn that copy may give a false idea.
old example: Riley said: This could be seen as misleading because you've used the word 'free' but buried the conditions in very small print. The ASA looks at the overall impression, not the technical accuracy. Rewrite the headline.
new example: This could be seen as misleading because the offer ends soon.

word: THIS IS SUBJECT TO [REGULATORY BODY] APPROVAL
old definition: A phrase used in briefings and timelines to signal that content must be reviewed and approved by a regulator before it can be used.
new definition: A way to say an official group must approve something first.
old example: 'The financial promotion copy is subject to FCA approval. We cannot include it in the media plan until we have a formal clearance letter. Build an extra week into the timeline.'
new example: The new savings advert is subject to FCA approval.

old definition: A short, structured public talk (usually 10-18 minutes) built around one clear idea — designed to be compelling enough to share widely.
new definition: A short public talk built around one big idea.
old example: Marcus said: The CMO wants to do a TED-style talk at the industry conference. Riley said: Then she needs one clear idea — not five. The whole talk should make the audience see something they couldn't see before.
new example: She gave a TED-style talk about the future of shopping.

old definition: The main speech at a conference or event — usually given by a senior or high-profile speaker. It sets the theme or direction for the whole event.
new definition: The main speech at a conference.
old example: Riley said: A keynote isn't just a big presentation. It's a statement of where the industry is going. The audience comes to understand what to think about next — not just what the speaker's company does.
new example: Our CEO will give the keynote on Monday.

old definition: A written declaration of beliefs, values, or intentions — usually bold and written to inspire others to believe or act the same way.
new definition: A bold statement of what you believe.
old example: The agency published a 2,000-word manifesto on why the age of mass advertising is over. It didn't just promote their services — it made an argument. And within a week, it had been shared more than 4,000 times.
new example: Our brand manifesto lists five promises.

old definition: A letter written to a specific person or group but published publicly — used to make a formal argument or challenge visible to a wide audience.
new definition: A letter to someone that everyone can read.
old example: Marcus wrote an open letter to the marketing industry about greenwashing. Riley said: An open letter is a power move — you're not just talking to the addressee, you're talking to everyone who reads it. Make sure the argument is airtight.
new example: The founder wrote an open letter to the industry.

old definition: A short opinion article published in a newspaper, magazine, or online platform — named after the page opposite the editorial page in print. Expresses a clear point of view.
new definition: A short opinion article in a newspaper or online.
old example: Riley said: An op-ed is different from a blog post. It has a clear argument, a news hook, and it takes a position most people either agree or disagree with strongly. That's what makes it shareable.
new example: His op-ed about AI got thousands of shares.

old definition: An observation or idea that the audience hasn\'t heard before — the core of all effective thought leadership. Without an original insight, you\'re just repeating what everyone already knows.
new definition: A new idea that people haven't heard before.
old example: Marcus said: I've read 40 articles about AI in marketing and they all say the same things. Riley said: That's exactly why you need an original insight — one perspective that reframes the whole conversation. What does everyone get wrong about AI in marketing?
new example: Great talks need at least one original insight.

old definition: A clear, specific position on a topic — often used in strategy documents, pitches, and thought leadership to signal that the speaker has a defined perspective, not just information.
new definition: A clear opinion on a topic.
old example: Riley said: Before we write the white paper, define the POV. What is the one sentence that expresses what we believe — that most people would either strongly agree or strongly disagree with? That's your POV. Everything else is evidence.
new example: Our point of view is that small brands can win.

old definition: The combination of channels and formats a person uses to consistently share their ideas — including speaking engagements, LinkedIn, published articles, podcasts, and interviews.
new definition: The channels you use to share your ideas.
old example: Marcus said: She's the smartest person in the room but no one outside this building knows it. Riley said: She needs a platform — one or two channels where she consistently publishes her thinking. Start with LinkedIn and one industry publication.
new example: LinkedIn is her main platform.

word: THE ONE IDEA IN THIS TALK IS...
old definition: A structuring phrase used when building a TED-style talk or keynote — great speakers commit to one central idea and build everything around it.
new definition: A way to state the main idea of a talk.
old example: 'The one idea in this talk is that brands that don't take a public position on cultural issues will lose the next generation of consumers. Everything else in the 15 minutes supports or proves that claim.'
new example: The one idea in this talk is that trust beats price.

word: WHAT I WANT THE AUDIENCE TO THINK DIFFERENTLY ABOUT IS...
old definition: A phrase used when designing a thought leadership piece — naming the specific belief or assumption you want to change.
new definition: A way to say what you want to change in people's minds.
old example: 'What I want the audience to think differently about is the relationship between creativity and performance marketing. Most people treat them as opposites. My argument is that they are inseparable — and the data proves it.'
new example: What I want the audience to think differently about is failure.

old definition: A classic thought leadership structure — name the idea everyone holds, then challenge it with your original insight.
new definition: A way to challenge a common belief.
old example: 'The conventional wisdom is that brand and performance are separate functions. But the data from the last five years shows that brands who separated them underperformed by 30% compared to those who kept them integrated.'
new example: The conventional wisdom is that email is dead, but it still works.

word: LET ME TELL YOU WHAT EVERYONE IN THIS ROOM IS GETTING WRONG
old definition: A bold opening phrase for a keynote or talk — immediately creates tension and signals that the speaker has an original perspective.
new definition: A bold way to start a talk.
old example: Riley said: You want to open strong? Start with: 'Let me tell you what everyone in this room is getting wrong about customer retention.' That's a hook. Now they have to listen to find out if they're guilty.
new example: Good morning. Let me tell you what everyone in this room is getting wrong.

word: THE QUESTION THIS PIECE ANSWERS IS...
old definition: A phrase used when pitching or opening a thought leadership article, op-ed, or manifesto — naming the specific question the piece exists to answer.
new definition: A way to say what an article is about.
old example: 'The question this piece answers is: why do most rebrands fail within three years? The short answer will surprise most brand managers — and the data behind it should change how every CMO approaches a rebrand.'
new example: The question this piece answers is why customers leave.

old definition: A phrase used in coaching or strategy conversations when advising someone on how to establish their thought leadership presence.
new definition: Advice to focus your public content on one topic.
old example: Marcus said: Where should she start? Riley said: Build her platform around one specific topic — not 'marketing' but 'how B2B brands can use emotion in marketing without losing credibility'. That's specific enough to own.
new example: Build your platform around one clear topic.

old definition: A framework by researcher Geert Hofstede that measures cultural differences across countries using six dimensions — such as individualism vs. collectivism and high vs. low power distance. Used by global brands to understand audiences.
new definition: A model that compares cultures in several ways.
old example: Riley said: Before we adapt the campaign for Japan, look at the Hofstede dimensions. Japan scores very high on collectivism — which means the messaging should focus on the community and shared values, not individual achievement.
new example: Hofstede dimensions show that Japan avoids risk more than the US.

old definition: The process of changing a campaign, product, or communication style to fit the values, expectations, and norms of a specific culture.
new definition: Changing a campaign to fit another culture.
old example: The original campaign showed a man making a solo decision without consulting his family. In the cultural adaptation for Korea, the scene was rewritten to show a group discussion — because individual decision-making without consultation felt unusual to that audience.
new example: The Asian campaign needed cultural adaptation.

old definition: A small but important difference in meaning, tone, or implication — often the difference between a message landing well and landing badly in a different culture.
new definition: A small but important difference in meaning.
old example: Marcus said: The word 'challenge' in English has a positive connotation — it implies opportunity. But the nuance in Portuguese is more negative — it implies difficulty. That single word was making the campaign feel discouraging in Brazil.
new example: Translators must understand every nuance.

old definition: An unwritten cultural rule or expectation that most people in a culture follow automatically — without it ever being stated directly.
new definition: An unwritten rule most people in a culture follow.
old example: In many parts of Northern Europe, an implicit norm in business communication is directness — saying what you mean with little context. In Japan, the same implicit norm is indirect communication — meaning is often conveyed without being stated.
new example: Arriving late is an implicit norm in some countries.

old definition: A culture where communication relies heavily on context, relationships, and what is left unsaid — meaning is not always stated directly.
new definition: A culture where much meaning is not said directly.
old example: Riley said: China is a high-context culture. A polite 'that is interesting' in a business meeting often means 'no'. Marketing copy that is too blunt or direct may come across as rude or unsophisticated.
new example: In a high-context culture, relationships come first.

old definition: A culture where communication is explicit and direct — people say what they mean and meaning is not usually hidden in context or relationships.
new definition: A culture where people say exactly what they mean.
old example: Germany is considered a low-context culture — business communication is expected to be direct, detailed, and clear. A campaign built on implication and suggestion may confuse or frustrate a German audience expecting clarity.
new example: The US is a low-context culture.

old definition: The full process of adapting a product, campaign, or communication for a specific local market — including language, visuals, values, pricing, and format.
new definition: Changing a product or message for a local market.
old example: Localisation is not just translation. McDonald's localises its entire menu for India — no beef, different spices, vegetarian options designed for local tastes. The brand is consistent; everything that touches the customer is local.
new example: Localisation means local prices, photos and language.

old definition: Awareness of and respect for cultural differences — especially the ability to avoid content that could offend or misrepresent a culture.
new definition: Respecting differences between cultures.
old example: The ad was pulled in three Middle Eastern markets due to a lack of cultural sensitivity — it showed behaviour that is considered deeply disrespectful in those countries. The brand issued a public apology and a full review of its global approval process.
new example: Cultural sensitivity stops us from making offensive ads.

old definition: A phrase used when a campaign element — a visual, a message, or a tone — has a different effect in one cultural context than in another.
new definition: A way to say something is understood differently in another country.
old example: 'The humour works in the UK because self-deprecation is endearing. But this plays differently in the US — American audiences often read it as low confidence rather than charm. We need to adjust the tone.'
new example: Be careful: this joke plays differently in Brazil.

word: WE NEED TO RUN THIS THROUGH A LOCAL LENS
old definition: A phrase used in global marketing teams to flag that content must be reviewed by someone with local cultural knowledge before it is approved.
new definition: A way to say local people should check the content.
old example: Marcus said: Before we approve the campaign for Southeast Asia, we need to run it through a local lens. Riley said: Agreed — our local teams in Singapore and Bangkok should review the visuals and copy. Cultural sensitivity reviews are non-negotiable for this region.
new example: Before we launch, we need to run this through a local lens.

word: THE MESSAGE GETS LOST IN TRANSLATION — NOT JUST LINGUISTICALLY BUT CULTURALLY
old definition: A phrase used to describe when the cultural meaning or emotional impact of a campaign doesn\'t transfer between markets, even if the language is accurately translated.
new definition: A way to say the meaning changes in another culture.
old example: 'The concept works perfectly in English — the warmth and the self-awareness are very British. But the message gets lost in translation — not just linguistically but culturally — when it moves to markets where that kind of irony isn't familiar.'
new example: The message gets lost in translation — not just linguistically but culturally.

old definition: A phrase used when briefing a team or agency to make sure they understand the unwritten cultural rules that govern how people communicate and behave in a specific market.
new definition: A reminder to follow unwritten local rules.
old example: 'When building the campaign for Japan, respect the implicit norms of the culture — harmony, group identity, and restraint. Don't use direct calls to action that pressure the individual. Let the audience come to the conclusion themselves.'
new example: Respect the implicit norms of Japanese business meetings.

old definition: A core principle in global marketing — a reminder that effective market adaptation requires cultural change, not just linguistic conversion.
new definition: A rule to adapt content, not only change the language.
old example: Riley said: The brief says 'translate the campaign into Mandarin'. That's not enough — localise, don't just translate. The visuals, the values in the copy, the humour — all of it needs to be reconsidered for a Chinese audience.
new example: Localise, don't just translate: change the photos too.

word: THIS RISKS CULTURAL APPROPRIATION OR MISREPRESENTATION
old definition: A phrase used to flag content that takes elements from another culture inappropriately — without understanding, permission, or proper representation.
new definition: A warning that content may use another culture badly.
old example: Marcus said: The creative team wants to use traditional Maori imagery in the campaign. Riley said: This risks cultural appropriation or misrepresentation. We need to work directly with Maori cultural consultants — not just borrow visual elements from their culture.
new example: This dress design risks cultural appropriation or misrepresentation.

old definition: Recreating a message in another language so that it has the same emotional effect — rather than translating it word for word. The meaning may change, but the feeling and impact stay the same.
new definition: Recreating a message in another language with the same feeling.
old example: Riley said: We can't translate 'Just Do It' literally into Arabic and expect it to land. Transcreation means finding the phrase that creates the same feeling of confidence and urgency in Arabic — even if the words are completely different.
new example: The slogan needed transcreation for the French market.

old definition: Translating a document back into the original language — used to check whether the translated version says what was intended, and hasn\'t shifted in meaning.
new definition: Translating a text back to the first language to check it.
old example: Marcus said: The German version of the campaign line came back very differently from the original. Riley said: That's why we always run a back-translation. If the back-translation doesn't match the brief, the translation has drifted.
new example: The back-translation showed a big mistake.

old definition: A document given to the translation or creative team that explains the intent, tone, cultural context, and specific instructions for adapting content to a new market.
new definition: A document that explains how to adapt content for a market.
old example: Riley said: Never send copy to a translator without a localisation brief. They need to know who the audience is, what emotional response you're trying to create, which phrases can't be changed, and which cultural references to avoid.
new example: Send the localisation brief to the Spanish team.

old definition: A review of all the language used across a brand\'s communications — to check for consistency, accuracy, tone of voice, and quality across markets.
new definition: A check of all the words a brand uses.
old example: The language audit revealed that three of our markets were using an outdated product name that was discontinued two years ago. Another market had translated the brand tagline in a way that changed the meaning entirely. This is why you audit.
new example: The language audit found three different names for one product.

old definition: A controlled list of approved translations or terms for a brand — ensuring that key words, product names, and phrases are always translated the same way.
new definition: A list of approved words and translations for a brand.
old example: Marcus said: Every market is translating 'customer success' differently — some say 'client victory', others say 'customer achievement'. Riley said: That's a glossary problem. Once the brand glossary is agreed, every translation agency uses it. No exceptions.
new example: Check the glossary before you translate product names.

old definition: The brand\'s character and style expressed in language — maintained across multiple languages even though the words are different.
new definition: The brand's style of speaking in every language.
old example: Our tone of voice is warm, direct, and a little irreverent. That translates differently in French than in Spanish. The French version needs to be more sophisticated; the Spanish version can be more informal. Same tone, different expression.
new example: Our tone of voice is friendly in every language.

old definition: Finding a reference, example, or expression in the target culture that creates the same meaning or emotional response as the original — rather than translating the original literally.
new definition: Finding a local idea that has the same effect.
old example: Riley said: The original copy uses a cricket analogy to describe a difficult situation. For the US market, we used a baseball equivalent. For Japan, we used a kendo reference. That's cultural equivalence — same meaning, culturally familiar example.
new example: For cultural equivalence, we changed baseball to football.

old definition: A document that defines how the brand should be written in each language — including tone, formatting, approved terms, and cultural guidelines for each market.
new definition: A guide that explains how to write the brand in each language.
old example: Marcus said: We have a style guide in English — do we need one in every language? Riley said: If you want consistency across 12 markets, yes. The multilingual style guide is what keeps the brand voice from drifting market by market over time.
new example: The multilingual style guide covers six languages.

old definition: A phrase used when a piece of copy is too creative, idiomatic, or emotionally dependent to be translated literally — it needs to be recreated in the target language.
new definition: A way to say the text must be rewritten, not just translated.
old example: 'The strapline, the puns in the body copy, and the cultural references all need transcreation, not translation. If we translate these literally, the humour disappears and the emotional impact is completely lost.'
new example: This joke won't work in German. This needs transcreation, not translation.

old definition: An instruction to translate a completed translation back into the original language — to verify whether the meaning was preserved.
new definition: An instruction to translate a text back to check its meaning.
old example: 'Before we approve the Italian copy, run a back-translation to check that the key messages haven't drifted. Last quarter the Spanish version changed the emotional tone entirely — we didn't catch it until the campaign was live.'
new example: Run a back-translation to check the safety message.

word: BRIEF THE TEAM WITH A LOCALISATION BRIEF
old definition: An instruction to prepare and share a structured document that gives translators and local creative teams everything they need to adapt content correctly.
new definition: An instruction to give the team clear adaptation notes.
old example: Riley said: Before we brief the agency in Seoul, brief the team with a localisation brief. Include the target audience profile, the brand voice description in Korean, the list of locked phrases, and the cultural considerations. Don't assume they know what we know.
new example: Brief the team with a localisation brief before they start.

word: MAINTAIN THE TONE OF VOICE ACROSS LANGUAGES
old definition: A goal or instruction in multilingual marketing — ensuring that the brand\'s personality comes through even when the words are in a completely different language.
new definition: A rule to keep the same brand style in every language.
old example: 'The challenge is to maintain the tone of voice across languages. In German, 'direct and confident' sounds different from the same quality in Italian or in Japanese — but the underlying character should be recognisably the same brand.'
new example: Maintain the tone of voice across languages, so we always sound friendly.

old definition: An instruction to use the approved translation for a specific word or phrase — rather than leaving it to the translator\'s discretion.
new definition: An instruction to use the approved translation of a word.
old example: 'For the product name, use the brand glossary — there are approved translations in 14 languages and we need consistency. Do not create new translations at market level.'
new example: Use the brand glossary for 'smart home'.

old definition: An instruction to replace a reference, example, or idiom with one that has the same meaning or resonance in the target culture.
new definition: An instruction to find a local example that works the same way.
old example: 'The analogy in the English copy references the Tube — which means nothing in the US. Find the cultural equivalent in the US market. Something like 'a crowded subway car' or 'rush hour on the Metro' would land the same way.'
new example: Find the cultural equivalent in Japan for this holiday.

old definition: The ethical idea that the right action is the one that produces the greatest benefit for the greatest number of people. In marketing, it\'s often used to justify decisions that help most customers even if they disadvantage a few.
new definition: The idea that the right action helps the most people.
old example: Riley said: The targeting algorithm works for 95% of users — it shows them relevant content. But it over-exposes the remaining 5% to gambling ads. A utilitarian would say the net benefit justifies it. I'm not sure I agree.
new example: Utilitarianism says the free test helps more people than it harms.

old definition: The ethical idea that the right action is the one that a person of good character would take. Instead of asking "what produces the best outcome?", it asks "what kind of company do we want to be?"
new definition: The idea of doing what a good person would do.
old example: Marcus said: Forget the legal question — ask the virtue ethics question. If we run this campaign, what does it say about us as a company? Would the people we respect most in this industry be proud of it?
new example: Virtue ethics asks if an honest company would run this advert.

old definition: Influencing someone\'s decision through means that bypass their rational thinking — such as creating false urgency, exploiting emotions, or hiding important information.
new definition: Influencing people in an unfair or hidden way.
old example: Riley said: Using a countdown timer on a product that never actually runs out of stock is manipulation — it creates false urgency. Persuasion is fine. Persuasion that bypasses the customer's ability to think clearly crosses an ethical line.
new example: Fake countdown timers are a form of manipulation.

old definition: The customer\'s right to make their own free and informed decisions. Ethical marketing respects customer autonomy — it informs and persuades, but doesn\'t override the ability to choose.
new definition: A person's right to make their own choices.
old example: Marcus said: The dark pattern design is engineered to trick users into signing up for a subscription they didn't want. That violates their autonomy. Riley said: Exactly — and it's increasingly illegal under consumer protection law, not just ethically wrong.
new example: Clear prices respect customer autonomy.

old definition: Explicit agreement from a customer to be contacted, have their data used, or receive a specific type of communication — freely given and clearly informed.
new definition: Clear permission from someone.
old example: Consent under GDPR must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. Pre-ticked boxes are not consent. A blanket terms and conditions document is not consent. A clear 'Yes, I would like to receive marketing emails' checkbox is consent.
new example: We need consent before we send marketing emails.

old definition: A design or interface choice intentionally created to trick users into doing something they didn\'t intend to do — like signing up for a service, sharing more data, or making a purchase.
new definition: A website design that tricks people.
old example: Riley said: The unsubscribe flow has seven steps and the confirmation button is grey on a grey background. That's a dark pattern. The intent is to make it so difficult to unsubscribe that people give up. It's legal in some markets but it's ethically indefensible.
new example: A hidden 'cancel' button is a dark pattern.

old definition: Taking advantage of someone\'s vulnerability, fear, or lack of knowledge to influence their behaviour — in a way they would object to if they were fully aware of it.
new definition: Taking unfair advantage of people.
old example: Marketing to people in financial difficulty with high-interest credit products is exploitation — it targets people when they are least able to make good decisions and most likely to make harmful ones. The law is beginning to catch up with this, but many practices remain technically legal.
new example: Selling loans to people in debt can be exploitation.

old definition: Being open and honest with customers about what your product is, how it works, what it costs, and how their data is used — without hiding important information in fine print.
new definition: Being open and honest.
old example: Marcus said: The pricing on the website is transparent — you see the full cost before you check out. No hidden fees discovered at the end. Riley said: That's the minimum standard. True transparency means the customer understands what they're agreeing to, not just that the information was technically available.
new example: Transparency about fees builds trust.

word: WHERE IS THE LINE BETWEEN PERSUASION AND MANIPULATION?
old definition: A question used to open a discussion about whether a specific marketing practice respects or exploits the customer\'s ability to decide freely.
new definition: A question about when marketing becomes unfair.
old example: 'Where is the line between persuasion and manipulation? A compelling story that makes someone want your product is persuasion. A countdown timer on a product that never actually runs out is manipulation — it creates a false belief that overrides rational choice.'
new example: This advert uses fear. Where is the line between persuasion and manipulation?

old definition: A phrase used to evaluate whether a marketing practice allows customers to make genuine, informed choices or interferes with their ability to do so.
new definition: A way to say if a practice lets people choose freely.
old example: 'A clear price comparison page with genuine alternatives respects customer autonomy — it gives people what they need to choose. A pre-selected add-on in the checkout that requires active effort to remove violates customer autonomy — it makes the default choice for you.'
new example: Auto-renewal without warning violates customer autonomy.

word: THE UTILITARIAN CASE FOR THIS IS...
old definition: A phrase used to articulate the argument that a practice is justified because it produces the greatest benefit overall — even if it has some negative effects.
new definition: A way to argue that something helps the most people.
old example: 'The utilitarian case for personalised advertising is that it shows relevant products to people who genuinely want them and reduces wasted exposure. The counterargument is whether the benefit to the majority justifies the privacy cost to all.'
new example: The utilitarian case for this is that thousands save money.

word: WHAT WOULD A COMPANY OF GOOD CHARACTER DO HERE?
old definition: A virtue ethics framing question — used to evaluate a decision based on what it says about the company\'s values, rather than what is legally permitted or financially optimal.
new definition: A question to check if something is the right thing to do.
old example: Riley said: Forget what is legal. Forget what the competitors are doing. Ask a virtue ethics question: what would a company of good character do here? If the answer is different from what we're doing, we have a problem.
new example: Before we decide, what would a company of good character do here?

word: THIS CROSSES AN ETHICAL LINE BECAUSE...
old definition: A phrase used to explain why a specific practice goes beyond what is acceptable — with a clear reason.
new definition: A way to explain why something is wrong.
old example: 'Targeting users who have recently searched for addiction recovery services with alcohol ads crosses an ethical line because it deliberately targets people in a vulnerable state with content that is actively harmful to them. The fact that it is legal doesn't make it acceptable.'
new example: This crosses an ethical line because it targets children.

word: IS THE CUSTOMER MAKING A FREE AND INFORMED CHOICE?
old definition: A direct test for whether a marketing practice respects customer autonomy — used to evaluate everything from data consent to pricing design.
new definition: A question to check if customers really understand what they agree to.
old example: 'Before we launch the checkout flow, ask this: is the customer making a free and informed choice? Do they understand what they're buying, what they're agreeing to, and what happens next? If the answer is no, we need to redesign before we go live.'
new example: With hidden fees, is the customer making a free and informed choice?

old definition: The meaning beneath the surface of what is said — the real message behind the words.
new definition: The hidden message under someone's words.
old example: When the CEO said 'we value our current partners', the subtext was clear to everyone in the room: we are not looking for new agencies right now.
new example: The subtext of his email was 'hurry up'.

old definition: The language and conversation that surrounds a topic in society — the shared way people talk and think about an issue.
new definition: The way people usually talk about a topic.
old example: The discourse around AI in marketing has shifted from fear about job losses to curiosity about what's possible. Language shapes that shift as much as the technology itself.
new example: The public discourse about AI is changing fast.

old definition: Related to a legal duty to act in someone else\'s best financial interest — typically used to describe the responsibility of a board to shareholders.
new definition: About the legal duty to protect someone's money.
old example: The board has a fiduciary duty to shareholders — every major decision, including the rebrand budget, must be justifiable in terms of long-term financial value.
new example: Directors have a fiduciary duty to investors.

old definition: Recreating a message in another language so that it has the same emotional effect — rather than translating it word for word.
new definition: Recreating a message in another language with the same feeling.
old example: The campaign line needed transcreation for the Japanese market — the wordplay in English simply doesn't exist in Japanese, so the team wrote a completely new line that created the same feeling.
new example: Our slogan needed transcreation for Brazil.

old definition: Influencing someone\'s decision through means that bypass their rational thinking — such as false urgency, emotional exploitation, or hidden information.
new definition: Influencing people in an unfair way.
old example: A countdown timer on a product that never runs out is manipulation — not persuasion. The distinction matters both ethically and legally.
new example: Fake reviews are a clear example of manipulation.

old definition: The physical thing you see, hear, or read — the image, word, or symbol that carries a meaning.
new definition: The thing you see or hear, like a picture or word.
old example: The golden arches are the signifier. The meaning of warmth, reliability, and convenience that they create — that is the signified. Both are part of the brand's semiotic system.
new example: The crown in the logo is a signifier of quality.

old definition: Your brand\'s advertising spend as a percentage of all advertising spend in the category.
new definition: Your share of all the advertising in your market.
old example: Our share of voice is 18% but our market share is 25%. We are underinvesting relative to our market position — that gap will show in brand metrics within 12 months.
new example: Our share of voice grew to 25%.

old definition: The customer\'s right to make their own free and informed decisions without being manipulated or deceived.
new definition: A person's right to make their own choices.
old example: Dark patterns violate customer autonomy — they use design to override the customer's ability to make a genuine choice. Ethical marketing persuades; it doesn't manipulate.
new example: Honest prices respect customer autonomy.

old definition: A phrase used to introduce a new perspective on an issue — presenting the same situation in a way that changes how the listener thinks about it.
new definition: A way to say the same idea in a better way.
old example: 'Let me reframe that. You said the campaign underperformed. I'd say the campaign tested a new channel and gave us data that's worth £50k in avoided future mistakes. That's a different story.'
new example: Let me reframe that: it's a challenge, not a crisis.

old definition: A phrase used to redirect a conversation away from a surface-level issue to the underlying decision or challenge.
new definition: A way to move to the most important question.
old example: 'The real question here is not whether the campaign was creative. The real question is whether it moved the metrics that matter for the business. Let's look at the data.'
new example: The real question here is what customers need.

old definition: A core principle of global marketing — effective market adaptation requires rethinking content culturally, not just converting the language.
new definition: A rule to adapt content, not just change the language.
old example: 'Localise, don't just translate. The French market has different cultural values, a different visual register, and a different relationship to authority. A translated version of the English ad is not a local ad — it's an English ad in French.'
new example: Localise, don't just translate: change the examples too.

word: THIS CROSSES AN ETHICAL LINE BECAUSE...
old definition: A phrase used to explain clearly why a specific practice goes beyond what is acceptable — with a reason.
new definition: A way to explain why something is wrong.
old example: 'Targeting users who searched for mental health support with commercial advertising crosses an ethical line because it deliberately exploits vulnerability for commercial gain. That's not persuasion — it's exploitation.'
new example: This crosses an ethical line because it hides the real price.

old definition: A thought leadership structure — naming the widely held idea and then challenging it with original insight.
new definition: A way to challenge a common belief.
old example: 'The conventional wisdom is that you need a large budget to build a strong brand. But our analysis of challenger brands over ten years shows that consistency of message matters more than size of spend — by a factor of three.'
new example: The conventional wisdom is that young people don't read, but they do.

word: WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE IS...
old definition: A phrase used to translate data, analysis, or abstract findings into concrete business impact.
new definition: A way to explain what an idea means in real life.
old example: 'Customer satisfaction has dropped 8 points. What this means in practice is we're losing approximately 200 customers a month to the competitor — that's £1.4m in annual revenue if we don't act now.'
new example: What this means in practice is shorter emails.

old definition: Anything that gives you an advantage in a negotiation — a competing offer, a deadline the other party faces, specific expertise, or a large contract volume. Understanding your leverage and theirs is the first step in any commercial negotiation. Knowing your leverage does not mean threatening people with it — it means using it wisely.
new definition: Something that gives you an advantage when you negotiate.
old example: Riley assessed the situation before the meeting: What's our leverage here? We have two competitive quotes for the same media placement, we're committing to a 12-month contract upfront, and we can offer them a case study. That's three pieces of leverage — the volume commitment, the competitive alternatives, and the marketing value of our brand association.
new example: A better offer from another company gives us leverage.

old definition: Something you give up or agree to in a negotiation to move the deal forward or get something else you want more. Good negotiators never give concessions for free — every concession should come with a condition ('I can do that if you can...') and be traded, not simply handed over.
new definition: Something you agree to give up to help reach a deal.
old example: Marcus flagged the pattern: We've made three concessions in this negotiation and received nothing in return. That's not how this works. From now on, every concession we make must be conditional: 'I can move on the payment terms if you can commit to an extended contract length.' Always trade concessions; never give them for free.
new example: We made one concession: free delivery.

old definition: An offer you make in response to the other party's proposal — usually changing some of the terms rather than accepting or rejecting outright. A counter-offer keeps the conversation moving and shows you are still interested. Always counter rather than simply say no — 'no' ends the discussion, a counter-offer redirects it.
new definition: A new offer you make after hearing the other side's offer.
old example: Dana advised the team: They've come back with a 20% price increase on the renewal. Don't reject it — make a counter-offer. 'We can't move to that price point, but we could accept a 7% increase if you agree to lock in the rate for two years.' A counter-offer keeps us in the conversation and gives them a reason to keep negotiating.
new example: They asked for £10,000, so we made a counter-offer of £8,000.

old definition: An outcome that creates real value for both sides — not a win-lose result, but a deal where both parties get something meaningful. In long-term partnerships, mutual benefit matters because you want the other side to feel the deal was fair. A partner who feels shortchanged will not be motivated to deliver.
new definition: A result that is good for both sides.
old example: Riley framed the opening: I want to start by being clear about what we're both trying to achieve. We want a committed media partner who will deliver reach into the financial services sector. You want a flagship B2B client whose brand adds credibility to your platform. There's mutual benefit here — let's build an agreement that works for both of us.
new example: This partnership is a mutual benefit for both brands.

old definition: The specific conditions of an agreement — payment schedule, contract length, scope of work, deliverables, exclusivity, termination clauses. 'Agreeing terms' means finalising all the conditions before signing. In a negotiation, price is just one term — there are usually many others to discuss.
new definition: The conditions of an agreement.
old example: Marcus reviewed the negotiation priorities: Price is important, but it's not the only term we need to get right. Payment terms matter too — net-30 versus net-60 is a significant cash flow difference. And the exclusivity clause — if they can't guarantee category exclusivity, the deal is worth less than it looks on paper. Let's be clear about which terms we'll fight for and which we'll trade.
new example: We agreed on the terms: twelve months and monthly payments.

old definition: The point at which a deal is no longer good enough and you are prepared to walk away. Also called the BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement. You must know your walk-away point before the negotiation starts. Without it, you risk accepting terms that do not serve you.
new definition: The point where a deal is not good enough for you.
old example: Dana briefed the team before the meeting: Our walk-away point on this one is clear. If they can't commit to a 6-month minimum contract and won't include the retargeting placement in the base price, the deal doesn't work for us financially. We have a competing offer that's 15% cheaper. They need to know we're serious — but only if the conversation reaches that point.
new example: Our walk away point is £5,000 a month.

old definition: In negotiation, the first number or offer put on the table — which tends to set the tone for everything that follows. The party who puts the first number out there often has an advantage, because everything else in the conversation happens relative to that number. A strong opening anchor can change the whole range of possible outcomes.
new definition: The first number or offer that guides the rest of the talk.
old example: Riley explained the strategy: We're going to open with a lower anchor than we actually need. If we ask for a 12-month deal at a 15% discount, we have room to trade up to an 8% discount without feeling like we've given anything away. The party who sets the anchor first often ends up closer to their preferred outcome — so we open first.
new example: Their first price was a high anchor.

old definition: A situation in a negotiation where neither party can agree and nothing is moving forward. When you reach deadlock, you need something to break it — bring in a new variable, take a short break, look at the problem differently, or bring in a more senior decision-maker from one side.
new definition: When neither side can agree and talks stop.
old example: Marcus recognised the pattern: We've been going back and forth on price for 40 minutes and we're in deadlock. Let's take a different approach — instead of price, let's talk about what we each need the deal to include. When we agree on the shape of the deal, the price conversation becomes easier. Deadlock on one variable doesn't mean the whole deal is dead.
new example: After two hours, the talks reached a deadlock.

word: I CAN MOVE ON THAT IF YOU CAN MOVE ON...
old definition: The key phrase for trading concessions in a negotiation. 'Move on' means to be flexible or accept a change on a specific term. This is a conditional concession — you are offering flexibility on one thing in exchange for flexibility on something else. Never give a concession without this kind of condition attached.
new definition: A way to offer a change if the other side also changes something.
old example: Riley made the trade: I can move on the payment terms — we can do net-60 instead of net-30 if you can move on the contract length. Instead of 12 months, I need you to commit to 18. That way we both give something and both get something. That's the right structure for a trade.
new example: I can move on that if you can move on the start date.

word: LET'S FIND SOMETHING THAT WORKS FOR BOTH OF US
old definition: Use this phrase to steer a negotiation back toward a shared goal when it has become tense or stuck. It shows you are not trying to beat the other side — you want a deal that both parties can genuinely commit to. It helps lower the temperature and refocus on what matters to both of you.
new definition: A way to bring the talk back to a shared goal.
old example: Marcus de-escalated the conversation: I can see we're getting stuck on individual terms and losing sight of the bigger picture. Let's step back. We both want this partnership to work — it creates value for both organisations. Let's find something that works for both of us and stop treating this like a zero-sum game.
new example: We both want this deal, so let's find something that works for both of us.

word: THAT'S NOT SOMETHING WE CAN AGREE TO, BUT WHAT WE COULD DO IS...
old definition: A professional way to say no to one specific thing without ending the negotiation. Instead of a flat 'no', this phrase immediately offers an alternative. Use it when the other party proposes something outside what you can accept — you turn down the specific ask but give them a path forward.
new definition: A polite way to say no and offer another idea.
old example: Dana responded to the pricing demand: A 20% price increase is not something we can agree to — it's outside our approved budget and changes the economics of the partnership. But what we could do is accept a 9% increase now, with a commitment to revisit in 12 months based on the performance data. That gives you more than you have today and gives us the certainty we need.
new example: That's not something we can agree to, but what we could do is offer a discount.

word: WHAT WOULD NEED TO HAPPEN FOR YOU TO ACCEPT...
old definition: A question used to find out exactly what the other party needs in order to say yes to your proposal. It moves the conversation away from positions ('I want X') to underlying needs ('what I actually need is Y'). The answer often opens up a way to meet their need without giving up what you need.
new definition: A question to find out what the other side needs to say yes.
old example: Riley asked: You've said the timeline is the main issue. What would need to happen for you to accept a six-month delivery timeline rather than three months? The answer told us exactly what they needed — an additional resource commitment from our side in month one. We agreed to that, and the timeline issue was resolved.
new example: What would need to happen for you to accept a two-year contract?

word: I WANT TO BE TRANSPARENT ABOUT WHERE WE STAND
old definition: Use this phrase to share clear, honest information about your position or limits in a negotiation. Being open about your real constraints often encourages the other side to share theirs — which can open up solutions that neither party had thought of. Honesty, used well, speeds deals up.
new definition: A way to say you will be honest about your position.
old example: Marcus opened the renegotiation: I want to be transparent about where we stand. Our budget for this partnership was set before the market shift and we simply can't absorb a 20% increase without reducing scope elsewhere. I'd rather be honest about that now than agree to something we'll struggle to honour. Can we work within these parameters?
new example: I want to be transparent about where we stand: our budget is fixed.

word: WE'RE AT OUR LIMIT ON THAT ONE
old definition: A clear, direct phrase that signals you cannot go any further on a specific term — you have reached your limit on that point. Use it to stop the pressure on a term you genuinely cannot move on, without ending the whole conversation.
new definition: A way to say you cannot change something any more.
old example: Dana signalled the boundary: I want to keep this deal moving, but I need to be clear — on the exclusivity clause, we're at our limit. We cannot sign a deal that doesn't include category exclusivity for financial services. If that's a dealbreaker, we need to know now. But there may be other terms where we have more flexibility.
new example: Sorry, we're at our limit on that one; the price can't go lower.

old definition: Call to Action — the specific instruction that tells the reader what to do next: 'Book a demo', 'Download the guide', 'Start your free trial'. A good CTA is clear, specific, and gives the reader a reason to click. Weak CTAs like 'Learn more' or 'Click here' are too vague and people ignore them.
new definition: Short for call to action: words that tell the reader what to do next.
old example: Riley reviewed the landing page: The CTA at the bottom of this page says 'Submit'. That's the weakest possible call to action — it describes the mechanical action, not the value of taking it. Change it to 'Get your free audit'. Now the reader knows exactly what they're getting and it feels worth clicking.
new example: Our CTA says 'Start your free trial'.

old definition: The first and most prominent line of copy — the one that must stop the reader and make them want to keep reading. If the headline fails, the rest of the page is never read. The best headlines are specific, speak to a real need or fear, and promise a clear benefit.
new definition: The main line of text at the top of an advert or page.
old example: Dana rewrote the hero headline: 'Welcome to MarketBridge' is not a headline — it's a greeting. Nobody reads a landing page to be welcomed. Replace it with 'Cut your content approval time by 60%'. Now there's a specific, relevant, quantified benefit in the first line. That's a headline that makes someone read the next sentence.
new example: A strong headline makes people stop and read.
